Measure the tallest one every week.

quests.title: Decorate a hard-boiled egg
quests.why: An egg is a tiny blank canvas.
steps: A grown-up boils the egg and lets it cool.
Pens, paint or stickers.
Give it a face, a pattern or a name.

quests.title: Spring walk: find ten new green things
quests.why: Everything is waking up. Go and see.
steps: Grown-up along, out you go.
Look for new leaves, shoots, buds and moss.
Count ten different green things.

quests.title: Give one space a proper spring clean
quests.why: Spring is a good time to let the fresh air in.
steps: Pick one space: your desk, a shelf, the shoe pile.
Empty it, wipe it, sort it.
Put back only what belongs there.

quests.title: Three small kind things for three different people
quests.why: Kindness spreads. Today you start it.
steps: Pick three different people.
Do one small kind thing for each.
Tell Moss what you did, not them.

quests.title: Make a bookmark for your favourite book and tell someone why they should read it
quests.why: A good book is worth passing on.
steps: Make a bookmark with a picture from your favourite book.
Put it inside the book.
Tell someone the best bit, without giving away the end.

quests.title: Watch one patch of outdoors and count every creature you see
quests.why: There is more living out there than you think.
steps: Pick a patch with a grown-up: a hedge, a tree, a bit of park.
Watch it quietly for ten minutes.
Count every bird, bug and creature.

quests.title: Write a four-line poem about something you can see from a window
quests.why: Poems are just noticing, written down.
steps: Look out of a window for one minute.
Write four lines about one thing you see.
Read it to someone.

quests.title: Switch-off patrol: find five things left on and turn them off
quests.why: Every switch you flip saves a little energy.
steps: Walk the house with a grown-up.
Find lights, chargers and screens left on for no one.
Turn off five, and ask before anything you are unsure of.

quests.title: Teach a grown-up your best calm-down trick
quests.why: Grown-ups need calm tricks too.
steps: Pick the trick that works best for you.
Teach it to a grown-up, step by step.
Do it together once.

quests.title: Walk slowly, breathing in time with your steps
quests.why: A slow walk lets a big feeling drain out through your feet.
steps: Grown-up along, or round the garden.
Breathe in for four steps, out for four steps.
When you get back, tell a grown-up one word for how you feel.

quests.title: Animal walks: bear, crab and frog, one length each
quests.why: Animals never walk the boring way.
steps: Clear a long space.
Bear crawl there, crab walk back, frog jump there again.
Pick a new animal for the last length.

quests.title: Stand on one leg with your eyes shut and beat your time
quests.why: Balance is a quiet kind of strong.
steps: Stand on one leg, arms out.
Shut your eyes and count how long you last.
Three goes each leg. Beat your first time.

quests.title: Keepy-uppy with a balloon or a ball: beat your record
quests.why: Every extra touch is your feet getting cleverer.
steps: A balloon indoors, a ball outdoors.
Count how many touches before it drops.
Five goes. Beat your first score.

quests.title: Push the wall as hard as you can, ten slow times
quests.why: Pushing something that will not move helps your body calm down.
steps: Hands flat on a wall, feet back.
Push hard for five seconds, then let go.
Ten times, then tell a grown-up how you feel.

quests.title: Dance to three songs in a row without stopping
quests.why: Three songs is enough to shake a whole day off.
steps: Pick three songs you love.
Dance through all three. No sitting down.
Flop at the end and breathe.

quests.title: Play a game of tag with family or friends
quests.why: Nobody has ever stood still playing tag.
steps: Find players you know and a safe space, away from roads.
Agree the edges and the base.
Play until everyone has been it.

quests.title: Five slow stretches before bed, like a cat waking up
quests.why: Stretching tells your muscles the day is done.
steps: Reach up high, then fold down low.
Cat back, then cow back, on hands and knees.
Lie flat and stretch from fingers to toes.

quests.title: Kick a ball against a wall fifty times, left foot and right
quests.why: Your weaker foot gets better every time you use it.
steps: Find a safe wall with a grown-up's OK.
Twenty-five kicks with each foot.
Count how many come back to you.

quests.title: Walk to the post box or shop with a grown-up, the long way round
quests.why: The long way has more to look at.
steps: Pick a short errand with a grown-up.
Go the long way round.
Spot one thing you have never noticed before.

quests.title: Twenty catches in a row, then take a step back
quests.why: Catching is watching, and watching is a skill.
steps: Find someone to throw with, or use a wall.
Twenty catches without a drop.
Step back and go again.

quests.title: Sprint to a tree and back five times, resting in between
quests.why: Short, fast runs make you quicker than long, slow ones.
steps: Pick a tree or a marker in the garden, or at the park with a grown-up.
Sprint there and walk back.
Five times. Rest when you need to.

quests.title: Walk and talk: ten minutes with a grown-up, you choose the topic
quests.why: Walking side by side makes talking easier.
steps: Ask a grown-up to walk with you.
Pick the topic. Anything at all.
Ten minutes, then head home.

quests.title: Chalk a hopscotch and play it all the way through
quests.why: Hopscotch is hopping practice disguised as a game.
steps: Chalk the squares, one to ten, where a grown-up says is OK.
Throw a stone and hop the course.
Get all the way to ten.

quests.title: Balloon keep-up: fifty hits before it touches the floor
quests.why: A balloon is the slowest, silliest ball there is.
steps: A grown-up blows up a balloon. Clear some space.
Hands, heads, knees. Anything but catching.
Count to fifty without a drop.

quests.title: Roll down a grassy hill, then run back up
quests.why: Hills were made for rolling.
steps: Find a gentle grassy hill with a grown-up. Check the bottom is clear.
Lie sideways, arms in, and roll.
Run back up and do it again.

quests.title: Freeze dance: music on, freeze when it stops
quests.why: Stopping still is the hardest move of all.
steps: Ask someone to be in charge of the music.
Dance while it plays.
Freeze the second it stops. Wobble and you are out.

quests.title: Skipping rope: count your best run without tripping
quests.why: Skipping works everything, including your counting.
steps: Get a rope the right length: handles to your armpits.
Skip and count until you trip.
Five goes. Beat your best.

quests.title: Plank challenge: hold it, rest, then hold it longer
quests.why: Your middle holds the rest of you up.
steps: Forearms and toes, body straight.
Hold, then rest for the same time.
Three goes, each one longer.

quests.title: Set up a five-station circuit and do it twice
quests.why: Circuits get your whole body working without getting boring.
steps: Pick five moves: squats, star jumps, lunges, sit-ups, skips.
Thirty seconds each, a short rest in between.
Go round twice.

quests.title: Go for a ten-minute run without stopping
quests.why: Ten minutes non-stop is a real milestone.
steps: Agree the route with a grown-up. Under 13, run it with them.
Start slow. Slow enough to talk.
Keep going for ten minutes, however slowly.

quests.title: Build the tallest tower you can, then beat it
quests.why: Every tower teaches you how to build the next one.
steps: Use anything safe: blocks, cups, books, boxes.
Build as tall as you can before it falls.
Try again and beat it.

quests.title: Paper aeroplane contest: three designs, which flies furthest?
quests.why: Tiny changes make big differences. Test them.
steps: Fold three different planes.
Throw each one three times from the same spot.
Crown the one that flies furthest.

quests.title: Draw today as a four-box comic
quests.why: Every day has a story in it.
steps: Split a page into four boxes.
Draw the beginning, two middle bits and the end.
Add speech bubbles.

quests.title: Invent a brand new animal: draw it, name it, say what it eats
quests.why: Nobody has ever seen your animal before.
steps: Mix up two or three animals you know.
Draw it and give it a name.
Tell someone where it lives and what it eats.

quests.title: Make up a secret handshake and teach it to someone
quests.why: A handshake only two people know is a kind of club.
steps: Invent five moves: a clap, a bump, a wiggle.
Put them in order.
Teach it to someone until you both can do it fast.

quests.title: Play a board or card game and be a good winner or loser
quests.why: The best players are fun to play with, win or lose.
steps: Pick a game and a person.
Play it all the way through.
Shake hands at the end, whoever wins.

quests.title: Build a marble run from tubes and boxes
quests.why: Getting the slope just right is proper engineering.
steps: Collect tubes, boxes and tape.
Tape them down a wall or a pile of books.
Test it. Fix the bit where it gets stuck.

quests.title: Draw a map of an island that does not exist
quests.why: Every island starts as someone's idea.
steps: Draw the coastline any shape you like.
Add mountains, a forest, a beach, a secret place.
Give it a name and name three places on it.

quests.title: Make up a song about your day
quests.why: Singing about a day makes it yours.
steps: Pick a tune you know.
Change the words to be about today.
Sing it to someone, or just to yourself.

quests.title: Do a jigsaw or a puzzle for twenty minutes
quests.why: A puzzle quietens your head while your hands work.
steps: Pick a puzzle the right size for twenty minutes.
Edges first, then colours.
Stop at twenty minutes, or finish it.

quests.title: Doodle to music: draw whatever the song makes you think of
quests.why: Music can move your pencil for you.
steps: Put on a song you have not heard for a while.
Draw whatever comes, no rubbing out.
Try a different song on a new page.

quests.title: Make a creature from play dough or clay
quests.why: Squishing and shaping is good for busy hands.
steps: Warm the dough in your hands.
Make a creature with at least four parts.
Give it a name and a home.

quests.title: Play twenty questions at the table
quests.why: Yes or no is all you need to find anything.
steps: Think of something secret: an animal, a person, a thing.
Everyone asks yes or no questions.
Can they get it in twenty? Swap over.

quests.title: Invent a smoothie and give it a name
quests.why: Your smoothie, your name, your rules.
steps: Pick three things: fruit, yoghurt, milk, oats.
Blend it with a grown-up.
Name it and rate it out of ten.

quests.title: Plan your dream day, hour by hour
quests.why: Dreaming it up is half the fun.
steps: Write the hours down the side of a page.
Fill each one with something you would love.
Draw the very best bit.

quests.title: Make a mini golf course at home and play a round
quests.why: Nine holes, one living room, no rain.
steps: Make holes from cups and obstacles from books and tubes.
Use a soft ball and a rolled-up newspaper as a club.
Play a round and count your shots.

quests.title: Make a paper-bag puppet and give it a voice
quests.why: A puppet can say things you might not.
steps: Draw a face on a paper bag.
Add hair, ears, anything.
Give it a voice and let it tell a grown-up about your day.

quests.title: Colour hunt: snap ten things that are all the same colour
quests.why: Once you look for a colour, it is everywhere.
steps: Pick one colour.
Find ten things in that colour, inside or out.
Line them up or snap each one.

quests.title: Make a flip-book or stop-motion animation
quests.why: Moving pictures are just lots of still ones, very fast.
steps: Plan a tiny story: something moves from here to there.
Draw or shoot twenty frames, each one a bit different.
Flip it or play it back.

quests.title: Record a two-minute radio show
quests.why: Your voice, your music, your show.
steps: Plan it: a welcome, a song, a bit of news, a goodbye.
Record it on a phone with a grown-up's OK.
Play it to someone.

quests.title: Design your own trainers, T-shirt or logo
quests.why: Designers start with a pencil, like you.
steps: Pick what to design.
Sketch three ideas quickly.
Pick the best and draw it properly in colour.

quests.title: Design a video game level on paper
quests.why: Every game you love started on paper.
steps: Draw the level: start, finish, hazards, secrets.
Add three things to collect.
Talk someone through how to beat it.

quests.title: Write a short spooky story and read it with the lights low
quests.why: A little bit of spooky is fun when you are the one in charge.
steps: Pick a setting you know: your street, your school.
Write a one-page story with a twist.
Read it to someone with the lights down.

quests.title: Lie down and listen to one whole song with your eyes shut
quests.why: One song with your eyes shut is a tiny holiday.
steps: Pick a calm song.
Lie down somewhere comfy and shut your eyes.
Listen all the way to the end.

quests.title: Balloon breathing: fill your tummy like a balloon, then let it go slowly
quests.why: A slow balloon breath calms a fast heart.
steps: Hands on your tummy.
Breathe in slowly and make your tummy a big balloon.
Let it out slowly. Five balloons, then tell a grown-up how you feel.

quests.title: Bath or shower with no rush, then pyjamas early
quests.why: Warm water and early pyjamas make a heavy day lighter.
steps: Ask a grown-up for an early bath or shower.
Take your time. No rushing.
Straight into pyjamas and somewhere cosy.

quests.title: Relax each part of you in bed, from your toes to your face
quests.why: When every part of you is floppy, sleep comes easier.
steps: Lie still with the light off.
Squeeze and let go: toes, legs, belly, hands, shoulders, face.
Breathe slowly and stay floppy.

quests.title: Hug a soft toy or a pet and breathe slowly
quests.why: Holding something soft helps your body feel safe.
steps: Find your softest toy, or a pet who likes a cuddle.
Hold it close.
Five slow breaths, then tell a grown-up how you feel.

quests.title: Draw your worry, fold it up, and give it to a grown-up to keep
quests.why: A worry someone else is holding is lighter.
steps: Draw or write the worry.
Fold it up small.
Give it to a grown-up and tell them a bit about it.

quests.title: Fifteen minutes of colouring in
quests.why: Colouring in keeps your hands busy and lets your head rest.
steps: Pick a colouring page or draw your own shapes.
Colour slowly, inside the lines or not.
Stop at fifteen minutes.

quests.title: Listen to an audiobook or a story for fifteen minutes
quests.why: Someone else can do the reading today.
steps: Pick a story with a grown-up.
Get comfy somewhere quiet.
Listen for fifteen minutes.

quests.title: Blow bubbles as slowly as you can
quests.why: The slower you blow, the bigger the bubble, and the calmer you get.
steps: Get a bubble pot and wand.
Breathe in, then blow out very slowly.
Try to make the biggest bubble ever.

quests.title: Starfish breathing: trace your hand and breathe with each finger
quests.why: Five fingers, five slow breaths, one calmer you.
steps: Spread one hand like a starfish.
Trace up a finger breathing in, down breathing out.
All five fingers, then tell a grown-up how you feel.

quests.title: Lie down for twenty minutes after a big day
quests.why: Resting is not doing nothing. It is refilling.
steps: Find somewhere quiet and lie down.
No screens. Music or quiet.
Twenty minutes, even if you do not sleep.

quests.title: Watch the rain or the sky out of a window for five minutes
quests.why: Watching the sky for a while helps your own feelings settle.
steps: Find a window and a comfy spot.
Watch for five minutes. Count raindrops, clouds or birds.
Tell someone what you saw.

quests.title: Feed or water a pet or a plant without being asked
quests.why: Looking after something alive is a big job done in a small way.
steps: Check if they need food or water.
Give just the right amount.
Tell a grown-up it is done.

quests.title: Ask a grown-up: can I help? Then help with whatever they say
quests.why: Three words that make any job quicker.
steps: Find a grown-up in the middle of a job.
Ask: can I help?
Do the bit they give you, all the way to the end.

quests.title: Draw a picture for someone and deliver it
quests.why: A drawing just for them says: I thought of you.
steps: Pick someone who would like it.
Draw something they love.
Deliver it, with a grown-up if it is out of the house.

quests.title: Give someone a compliment that is not about how they look
quests.why: People remember being noticed for who they are.
steps: Notice something good someone did or is.
Tell them in one sentence.
Mean it.

quests.title: Sort the shoes by the front door into pairs
quests.why: Nobody likes hunting for the other shoe.
steps: Find every shoe by the door.
Match them into pairs.
Line them up neatly.

quests.title: Learn your address and a grown-up's phone number by heart
quests.why: Knowing it helps you get home if you ever get lost.
steps: Say your address slowly, a bit at a time.
Then a grown-up's phone number, in chunks.
Say both to a grown-up without looking.

quests.title: Wash your own hair at bath time
quests.why: One more thing you can do all by yourself.
steps: Wet your hair and use a small blob of shampoo.
Rub it all over, front to back.
Rinse with your eyes shut tight.

quests.title: Make a simple sandwich yourself, with a grown-up nearby
quests.why: Making your own food is a very grown-up thing.
steps: Get the bread and a filling you are allowed.
Spread it with a blunt knife.
Cut it with help, then clear up.

quests.title: Balance walk: heel to toe along a line, there and back
quests.why: Slow and steady is its own kind of strong.
steps: Lay a line on the floor: tape, string or a skipping rope.
Walk it heel to toe, arms out, there and back.
Now try it slower, then backwards.

quests.title: Make a picture with no pens: leaves, pasta, buttons, string
quests.why: Anything can be paint if you look at it right.
steps: Collect small things a grown-up says you can use.
Lay them out on paper to make a picture.
Give it a title, then tidy it all away.

quests.title: Lie still and listen for five different sounds
quests.why: Listening hard makes the rest of you go quiet.
steps: Lie down somewhere comfy and shut your eyes.
Count five sounds: near ones first, then far ones.
Tell a grown-up the quietest one you heard.

quests.title: Make a welcome-home sign for someone coming back today
quests.why: Being looked forward to is a lovely thing to come home to.
steps: Find out who is coming home next.
Draw a sign with their name and a picture.
Put it by the door before they arrive.

quests.title: Practise the Green Cross Code with a grown-up
quests.why: Knowing how to cross is a skill you use every day.
steps: Hold a grown-up’s hand and stop at the kerb.
Look both ways, then listen.
Tell them when you think it’s clear. They decide when you cross.

quests.title: Get the kitchen ready like a real kitchen crew
quests.why: Every cook starts with clean hands and a clear space.
steps: Sleeves up, long hair tied back, hands washed while you count to twenty.
Find where the chopping boards, bowls, spoons and tea towels live.
Clear and wipe the worktop so it is ready for cooking.

quests.title: Make a no-cook sharing plate that looks like a picture
quests.why: People eat with their eyes first.
steps: Ask who is eating, and check nobody is allergic to anything you want to use.
Wash the fruit and veg, then lay everything out as a picture: a sun, a boat, a smiley.
Put it in the middle and let everyone guess the picture.

quests.title: Wash and prep all the veg for tea
quests.why: Half of cooking is the getting ready.
steps: Ask which veg is going in tea tonight.
Scrub or rinse each one, and use a peeler once a grown-up has shown you how.
Tear, snap or pod them into a bowl, ready for the cook.

quests.title: Learn the bridge and the claw for safe cutting, a grown-up beside you
quests.why: Good cooks keep all their fingers. These two holds are how.
steps: A grown-up shows you the bridge: fingers one side, thumb the other, knife through the gap.
Then the claw: fingertips tucked in, knuckles guiding the knife.
Slice a cucumber or a soft fruit both ways, slowly, with your grown-up beside you.

quests.title: Make a sandwich lunch for the whole family
quests.why: Taking everyone's order is how real cooks start.
steps: Take everyone's order, and ask about allergies before you start.
Make each one the way they asked, and cut it with a table knife.
Serve it on plates with something crunchy and something fresh.

quests.title: Bake from a recipe: you read, weigh, mix and time it
quests.why: A recipe is a set of instructions. Follow it exactly and it works.
steps: Read the whole recipe first and get every ingredient out.
Weigh and mix it yourself. A grown-up does the oven, in and out.
Set the timer, check it is done, and copy the recipe onto a card for your cookbook.

quests.title: Cook eggs three ways on the hob, a grown-up beside you
quests.why: Eggs are the first thing most cooks learn. Three ways and you can make yourself a meal.
steps: A grown-up shows you the hob: pan handle turned in, oven gloves close, hob off when you finish.
On three days, cook eggs a new way: boiled, scrambled, then an omelette.
Rate each one and write your favourite on a recipe card.

quests.title: Cook a tomato sauce from scratch and serve it on pasta
quests.why: Once you can make one sauce, you can make a hundred meals.
steps: Chop an onion and a little garlic with the claw, a grown-up beside you.
Soften them in a pan, add tinned tomatoes and let it bubble gently for fifteen minutes, your grown-up still there.
Taste, season and serve it on pasta. A grown-up drains the hot water.

quests.title: Mix a no-cook dip, taste it and get the seasoning right
quests.why: Tasting as you go is what turns a recipe into your recipe.
steps: Ask who is eating and check for allergies. Mash a ripe avocado with a fork, or stir grated cucumber into yoghurt. A grown-up does the grating.
Add a squeeze of lemon and a tiny pinch of salt, then taste with a clean spoon.
Change one thing, taste again, then serve it with veg sticks for dipping.

quests.title: Make three no-cook breakfasts on three days
quests.why: Breakfast is the first meal most cooks make for themselves. These three need no heat at all.
steps: Day one, overnight oats: oats, milk and fruit stirred in a jar the night before.
Day two, a yoghurt pot layered with fruit. Day three, a cold plate of cheese, crackers, fruit and veg.
Rate each one and draw your favourite on a recipe card.

quests.title: Plan a three-course menu for a family meal
quests.why: Every good meal starts as a plan on paper.
steps: Ask everyone what they love, and anything they cannot eat.
Pick a starter, a main and a pudding that go together.
Write it out neatly, with a name for your restaurant.

quests.title: Check the cupboards, write the shopping list and find it all in the shop
quests.why: Cooks who check first never run out halfway through.
steps: Pick a meal to cook, then check what is already in the cupboards and fridge.
Write a list of what is missing, in the order you will find it in the shop.
In the shop with a grown-up, find every item and tick it off.

quests.title: Run a café lunch: three no-cook courses you make and serve
quests.why: A whole lunch on one table, with no heat needed.
steps: Day one: check allergies, plan three no-cook courses and make any that keep, like a dip or a pudding.
Day two: make the rest, a grown-up beside you for anything sharp.
Lay the table, hand out menus and serve one course at a time.

quests.title: Make your own kitchen cookbook of the things you can make
quests.why: A cookbook in your own writing is yours to keep.
steps: Gather your recipe cards, or write out three things you can now make.
Add a drawing to each one and a tip only you would know.
Make a cover and a contents page, then give a grown-up the tour.

quests.title: Draw your brave ladder: five things, smallest at the bottom
quests.why: Big brave things are small brave things stacked up.
steps: Think of five things that feel a bit scary, like asking to join a game or trying a club.
Draw a ladder and put the least scary one on the bottom rung.
Show a grown-up and choose the first rung to try.

quests.title: Find your brave voice: talk so the far end of the room hears
quests.why: A clear voice makes you feel braver, even before you are.
steps: Stand tall, feet apart, shoulders back.
Say your name and one thing you like to someone at the far end of the room.
Do it three times, slower and clearer each time.

quests.title: Say what you really think at tea, even if nobody agrees
quests.why: Your opinion counts, even when it is the only one.
steps: At tea, ask a question with lots of answers: best film, best pudding, best animal.
Give your real answer, even if everyone else says something different.
Give one reason, then listen to theirs.

quests.title: Say hello first to someone you know a little, on three days
quests.why: Saying hello first gets easier every time you do it.
steps: Pick someone you know a little: a child in your class, a lunchtime helper, a neighbour when you are out with your grown-up.
Say hello before they do, and use their name if you know it.
Three days, three hellos. Tell a grown-up about each one.

quests.title: Order for the whole table at a café, your grown-up beside you
quests.why: If you can order for everyone, you can order anywhere.
steps: Before you go, take everyone's order and practise saying it, allergies too.
At the counter or the table, with your grown-up right beside you, order for everyone.
Check it all arrived and say thank you.

quests.title: Ask to join a game that has already started
quests.why: Most games have room for one more. Somebody just has to ask.
steps: At school, a club or a family get-together, find a game you would like to join.
Wait for a gap, then ask: can I play too?
If it is a no, that is fine. Try another game, then tell a grown-up how it went.

quests.title: Introduce two people you know who have never met
quests.why: Introducing people is a confident thing to do, and anyone can learn it.
steps: At a visit or a family get-together, spot two people you know who have never met, like a friend and a grandparent.
Say each person's name, and one thing they have in common.
Stay for a minute to get them talking.

quests.title: Give a show-and-tell to someone who does not live with you
quests.why: Telling someone new about a thing you love is a brave kind of fun.
steps: Choose something that matters to you and plan three things to say about it.
Practise once to a toy, a pet or a mirror.
Show it to a relative or a family friend, then answer their questions.

quests.title: Give a new club three goes before you decide
quests.why: The first time is always the strangest. The third time tells you the truth.
steps: With a grown-up, choose a club or class you have never tried and find out what to bring.
Go along three times, and say hello to the leader each time.
After the third go, decide: stay, or try something else.

quests.title: Rehearse a short act for a bigger audience each day
quests.why: Each new person watching makes the next one easier.
steps: Pick a short act: a song, a poem, a trick, a joke or a dance.
Day one, perform it to a toy. Then to one person, then two, then everyone at home.
Each day, change one thing to make it better.

quests.title: Climb the top rung of your brave ladder
quests.why: Look how far down the bottom rung is now.
steps: Find your brave ladder, or draw a new one: five scary things, the scariest at the top.
Plan it with a grown-up: when, where and who will be there.
Do it, tick it off, then draw your next ladder.

quests.title: Make a feelings thermometer from one to five
quests.why: Knowing how big a feeling is helps you pick what to do about it.
steps: Draw a thermometer with five boxes, calm at the bottom and very big at the top.
Colour each box and write or draw how that number feels in your body.
Show a grown-up and say what number you are right now.

quests.title: Learn a new breath on three days and pick your favourite
quests.why: Different breaths suit different big feelings. Now you have three.
steps: Day one, square breathing: in for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four.
Day two, hot chocolate breathing: smell it slowly, blow it cool. Day three, hum like a bee as you breathe out.
Tell a grown-up which one worked best.

quests.title: Check your shoulders, hands and jaw three times today, and let them go
quests.why: Worry often shows up in your body before you notice it in your head.
steps: Three times today, stop and notice your shoulders, hands and jaw.
If they are tight, squeeze them a bit more, then let them go floppy.
At bedtime, tell a grown-up which part was tightest.

quests.title: Do everything in slow motion for five minutes
quests.why: A slow body tells a busy mind it can slow down too.
steps: Pick a job: walking to the kitchen, putting on socks, tidying a shelf.
Do it in slow motion, as slowly as you possibly can.
After five minutes, tell a grown-up how your body feels now.

quests.title: Make a calm-down jar and watch the glitter settle
quests.why: Feelings settle like the glitter, if you give them time.
steps: Fill a clean plastic bottle with warm tap water, a squeeze of clear glue and some glitter.
A grown-up seals the lid tight.
Shake it, then breathe slowly until every bit has settled.

quests.title: Choose a calm stone to keep in your pocket
quests.why: Something small to hold can help a big feeling shrink.
steps: With a grown-up, find a smooth stone in the garden or the park.
Wash it, and paint or draw on it if you like.
Hold it and take three slow breaths, rubbing your thumb across it each time.

quests.title: Draw your calm place, then visit it in your head
quests.why: You can go somewhere calm without moving at all.
steps: Think of a place, real or made up, where you feel calm.
Draw it, and add what you would hear, smell and feel there.
Shut your eyes and visit it in your head for two minutes.

quests.title: Write a calm sentence to say to yourself
quests.why: The words you say to yourself can calm you down.
steps: Think of what a kind friend would say when you are upset.
Turn it into one short sentence, like: this is big, and it will pass.
Write it on a card and say it slowly three times.

quests.title: Make a traffic light plan with a grown-up
quests.why: Planning for a big feeling on a calm day makes it smaller when it comes.
steps: Draw three lights: green for calm, amber for wobbly, red for very big feelings.
For each light, write what you notice in your body and what you will do.
Add what your grown-up can do to help on red, and stick it up.

quests.title: Practise two calm tricks on three calm days
quests.why: Fire drills happen on calm days. So do calm drills.
steps: Pick two calm tricks you like: a slow breath, squeezing and letting go, or a calm place in your head.
On a calm day, pretend a big feeling is coming and use them, start to finish.
Do it on three days, then tell a grown-up which one came most easily.

quests.title: Use a calm trick for real when a big feeling comes
quests.why: The practising was for this moment.
steps: When a big feeling arrives, give it a number from one to five, five the biggest.
Use one calm trick until the number drops.
Then tell a grown-up what happened and what helped.

quests.title: Make a map of the jobs that keep your home running
quests.why: Most jobs at home are invisible until you look for them.
steps: Walk round your home and spot ten jobs that need doing every week.
Write or draw each one, with who usually does it.
Circle one you could take on.

quests.title: Learn a new job from the person who usually does it
quests.why: Everyone does a job their own way. Learn it from the expert.
steps: Pick a job you have never done, like folding towels or emptying the dishwasher.
Ask the person who usually does it to show you, step by step.
Do it while they watch, then thank them for teaching you.

quests.title: Make a picture job card so anyone could do your job
quests.why: If you can explain a job, you really know it.
steps: Pick a job you can do well.
Draw each step in a box, in order, with a few words under each.
Ask someone to follow your card and see if it works.

quests.title: Get home ready for someone coming back from a long day
quests.why: Coming home to a ready house feels like a hug.
steps: Find out who is coming home, and roughly when.
Get their spot ready: shoes away, coats hung, a glass of water by their chair.
Leave a note saying you hope their day was good.

quests.title: Get everyone ready the night before: shoes, bags and coats
quests.why: A calm morning starts the night before.
steps: After tea, check what everyone needs tomorrow.
Line up the shoes in pairs, hang the coats and put the bags by the door.
Ask each person if anything is missing.

quests.title: Take on one family job every day for five days, no reminders
quests.why: A job you do every day is a job you own.
steps: Pick one daily job: feeding the pet, emptying the dishwasher, laying the table.
Do it every day before anyone has to ask.
Five days in a row. A grown-up checks: no reminders needed.

quests.title: Make a fair family job chart with everyone
quests.why: Jobs feel fairer when everyone helped decide.
steps: List the jobs that happen every week.
At a family meeting, agree who does which, so it is fair for everyone's age.
Draw the chart and stick it up where everyone sees it.

quests.title: Own one weekly job for four weeks
quests.why: Owning a job means nobody else has to think about it.
steps: Choose a weekly job with a grown-up: the recycling, the stairs, watering everything.
Do it on the same day each week, properly, with no reminders.
Four weeks done. Decide whether to keep it or swap.

quests.title: Invent a fix for a family muddle
quests.why: If something always goes missing, it needs a home.
steps: Spot a muddle that happens all the time: lost keys, a shoe pile, odd socks.
Invent a fix: a stick-on hook, a labelled box, a basket, a sign.
Set it up and show everyone how it works.

quests.title: Plan a family project, and give everyone a part
quests.why: A big job is lots of small jobs shared out.
steps: Choose a project with your grown-ups: clear the shed, plant a pot, sort the toy cupboard.
Write every job it needs, and what you will need to do it.
Give everyone a part that suits them, and pick a day.

quests.title: Do a family project together over a weekend
quests.why: Doing a big thing together is the best kind of tired.
steps: Take a before photo of the space.
Do your part and help others with theirs. Ladders, tools and strong cleaners are for grown-ups.
Clear up together and take an after photo.

quests.title: Swap at bedtime: you read the story to a grown-up
quests.why: Reading to someone is reading twice: once for the words, once for the voices.
steps: Pick a short book, or a few pages of a long one.
Read it to a grown-up at bedtime, voices and all.
Ask them which bit they liked best.

quests.title: Find the funniest joke in a joke book or comic and try it on three people
quests.why: A good joke is worth finding twice: once for you, and once for everyone you tell.
steps: Find a joke book, a comic or a funny story.
Pick the joke that made you laugh most and practise saying it.
Tell it to three people and see who laughs.

quests.title: Draw a new cover for a book you love
quests.why: A cover is a promise about what’s inside.
steps: Pick a book you love.
Design a new front cover: a picture, the title and who wrote it.
Show someone and tell them what you put on it, and why.

quests.title: Make up a new ending for a story you know
quests.why: Every story could have gone another way.
steps: Pick a story you know well: a book, a film or a fairy tale.
Change what happens at the end, then draw it or write it.
Share your ending with someone.

quests.title: Tell a story from the pictures in a picture book
quests.why: Pictures tell a story too, if you look closely.
steps: Pick a picture book, or a comic with lots of pictures.
Turn the pages and tell the story from the pictures, in your own words.
Ask a grown-up to read you what the words really say.

quests.title: Sit outside for five minutes and draw a map of every sound you hear
quests.why: Sit still for long enough and the world gets louder.
steps: Sit in the garden, on a doorstep or by an open window, with a grown-up near.
Draw yourself in the middle of the page, then each sound where it comes from.
Circle the quietest one you heard.

quests.title: Choose a tree near you and visit it on three days
quests.why: Look at one tree for long enough and it starts to feel like yours.
steps: Pick a tree you can get to with a grown-up: in the garden, the street or the park.
On three days, visit it. Feel the bark, look at the leaves and look for anything living on it.
Draw it, and add one thing that changed.

quests.title: Spot a bird, then find out its name
quests.why: Most of the birds you see every day have a name you could know.
steps: Go outside with a grown-up, or watch from a window.
Pick one bird. Notice its colours, its size and how it moves.
Find out its name from a book or a grown-up, and draw it.

quests.title: Make a nature table from five things found on a walk
quests.why: A walk you can keep.
steps: On a walk with a grown-up, pick up five things that have fallen: a leaf, a stick, a cone, a stone, a seed. No berries or mushrooms.
Lay them out at home and label each one.
Wash your hands, then tell someone where you found each one.

quests.title: Label every school thing you own
quests.why: Lost property is full of things with no name in them.
steps: Gather everything: jumper, coat, PE kit, bottle, lunchbox, bag.
Label each one with a grown-up: a name label, a sticker or a pen.
Check the jumper and the PE kit twice. They wander most.

quests.title: Do a practice school morning before term starts
quests.why: Doing it once before it counts makes the real day easier.
steps: Get up at your school-day time.
Get dressed in your uniform, have breakfast and get your bag ready.
Go the school route with a grown-up and see how long it takes.

quests.title: Draw your school week: PE days, library days and clubs
quests.why: Knowing what is coming makes each day feel easier.
steps: Find out what happens on each day of your school week.
Draw five boxes, one for each day, with a picture for PE, library or a club.
Stick it up and check it each night.

quests.title: Mark your lessons on a school map and learn the quickest routes
quests.why: In a big school, knowing where you are going is half of feeling settled.
steps: Get your timetable and a school map, from your planner or the school office.
Mark the rooms you go to most, plus the toilets, the library and the office.
Plan the quickest way between your trickiest pair of lessons, then try it on your next school day.

quests.title: Find three grown-ups at school you can go to for help
quests.why: Knowing who to ask is a big part of feeling settled.
steps: Think of the grown-ups at school: your teacher, a teaching assistant, the office, a lunchtime helper.
Pick three, and what you would go to each of them for.
Tell a grown-up at home their names and why you chose them.

quests.title: Learn one new name at school each day for five days
quests.why: People light up when you remember their name.
steps: Each day, find out the name of one person in your class or club you do not know yet.
Say hello to them using their name.
Five days, five names. Tell a grown-up at home who they are.

quests.title: Make a playtime plan B for when your friends are busy
quests.why: A plan B means there is always something to do.
steps: Think of three things you could do at playtime if your usual friends are busy or away.
Pick a game to ask to join, a club, or a calm spot to read or draw.
Tell a grown-up your plan B, and try it once this week.

quests.title: Empty your school bag every day and hand over every letter
quests.why: A letter at the bottom of a bag cannot help anyone.
steps: When you get home, empty your bag onto the table.
Every letter to a grown-up, lunchbox to the kitchen, kit in the wash.
Five school days running.

quests.title: Swap “how was school?” for a better question
quests.why: “How was school?” mostly gets “fine”. Better questions get stories.
steps: At tea, swap questions with a grown-up: what made you laugh today?
Listen to their whole answer before you give yours.
Try a new question on three days: what was hard, what surprised you.

quests.title: Shrink a school worry with a three-box plan
quests.why: A worry with a plan is smaller than a worry on its own.
steps: Draw three boxes: the worry, what might help, who could help.
Fill them in with a grown-up, drawing the worry as small as you can.
Pick one thing to try this week.

quests.title: Set up a homework spot that works
quests.why: A ready spot means less hunting for a pencil and more time for everything else.
steps: Choose a spot with a grown-up: a desk, or one end of the table.
Put everything you need in one pot or box: pencils, ruler, rubber, sharpener.
Agree a rule for screens while you work, and try it on your next homework.

quests.title: Find three things in common with someone new in your class
quests.why: Things in common are where friendships start.
steps: Pick someone you have not talked to much yet.
Ask questions until you find three things you both like.
Tell a grown-up at home what the three things were.

quests.title: Make a settled-in page about your first weeks
quests.why: Look back and see how much easier it has got.
steps: Write or draw: your teacher, a new friend, your favourite lesson, your best day so far.
Add one thing that felt hard at the start and is easier now.
Show a grown-up and keep it somewhere safe.

quests.title: Find three facts about a Black Briton from history and tell them at tea
quests.why: Black British history goes back hundreds of years. John Blanke played the trumpet for Henry VIII.
steps: Pick one: Mary Seacole, Walter Tull, Lilian Bader or John Blanke.
Find three facts with a grown-up, from a book or a museum website.
Tell your family at tea, without notes.

quests.title: Find out how the Windrush generation helped build modern Britain
quests.why: In June 1948 the Empire Windrush brought people from the Caribbean to help rebuild Britain. The NHS began two weeks later, and many went on to work in it.
steps: Find out what happened when the Empire Windrush arrived at Tilbury in 1948.
Find one person who came, and what they went on to do.
Tell a grown-up the part that surprised you most.

quests.title: Read a book by a Black British author or illustrator
quests.why: Malorie Blackman was the UK’s Children’s Laureate from 2013 to 2015.
steps: Ask a grown-up or a librarian for one: Malorie Blackman, Benjamin Zephaniah, Atinuke or Dapo Adeola.
Read it, or have it read to you.
Tell someone your favourite page and why.

quests.title: Perform a poem out loud with a beat, like Benjamin Zephaniah
quests.why: Benjamin Zephaniah, from Birmingham, wrote poems to be performed out loud, with a beat you can feel.
steps: Find a short poem: one of his, or one you write.
Clap the beat as you read it, until you know it.
Perform it to your family, standing up.

quests.title: Football practice, and the story of Walter Tull
quests.why: Walter Tull was one of England’s first Black professional footballers, and one of the first Black officers in the British Army.
steps: A ball, a wall and a grown-up nearby.
Ten passes against the wall with each foot, then five shots.
Tell your grown-up one thing about Walter Tull.

quests.title: Make a card for someone who keeps your community going
quests.why: This year’s theme is Honouring our Communities: the nurses, carers, teachers and volunteers people count on.
steps: Think of someone near you who helps: a nurse, a coach, a crossing patrol, a volunteer.
Make a card that says exactly what they do and why it matters.
Give it with a grown-up.

quests.title: Make a shaker and play along to calypso
quests.why: In 1959 Claudia Jones held an indoor Caribbean carnival in London. It helped inspire Notting Hill Carnival.
steps: Fill a clean plastic bottle a quarter full of dry rice or lentils, and a grown-up tapes the lid on tight.
Find calypso music with a grown-up and listen for the beat.
Shake along to one whole song, then teach the beat to someone at home.

quests.title: Look at the Moon with a grown-up, like space scientist Maggie Aderin-Pocock
quests.why: Dame Maggie Aderin-Pocock is a Black British space scientist. She has built parts for telescopes and presents The Sky at Night.
steps: On a clear evening, coat on, go outside with a grown-up.
Find the Moon and look at its shape. Binoculars help if you have them.
Draw what you see, and find out one thing Maggie Aderin-Pocock has worked on.

quests.title: Make an egg-box oware board and play a counting game from Ghana
quests.why: Oware is a counting game from Ghana, played across West Africa and in the Caribbean, where it’s often called warri.
steps: Use an egg box for six cups a side, with a pot at each end for each player’s store.
Put four beans, buttons or pebbles in every cup.
Learn the rules with a grown-up: scoop, drop one in each cup round the board, and capture when you make two or three. Play a full game.

quests.title: Plan a lantern face, then scoop while a grown-up carves
quests.why: Long before pumpkins, children in Scotland and Ireland carved Halloween lanterns out of turnips.
steps: Draw three lantern faces on paper and pick the friendliest.
A grown-up does all the cutting. You scoop out the seeds with a big spoon.
Light it with a battery tealight, never a real flame.

quests.title: Wash and roast your lantern’s seeds with a grown-up
quests.why: Lots of Halloween pumpkins are never eaten. The seeds are a snack in their own right.
steps: Rinse the seeds in a sieve and pick off the stringy bits.
Pat them dry, add a little oil and a pinch of salt or spice.
A grown-up roasts them until golden. Let them cool before you taste.

quests.title: Go guising at home: dress up and perform a party piece
quests.why: In Scotland, guisers earn their treat with a joke, a song or a poem, not a trick.
steps: Dress up from the dressing-up box.
Learn one joke, rhyme or song by heart.
Knock on a door at home and perform it for your grown-ups.

quests.title: Make a friendly monster mask from card
quests.why: Halloween means ‘hallowed evening’: the night before All Saints’ Day on 1 November.
steps: Draw a monster face on card. Friendly monsters only.
A grown-up helps you cut out the eye holes.
Add string, then give your monster a name.

quests.title: Pumpkin-spotting torch walk with a grown-up
quests.why: In lots of UK streets, a pumpkin in the window means trick-or-treaters are welcome to knock.
steps: Coat on, torch on, a grown-up beside you.
Walk your street and count every pumpkin in a window.
Pick the best one and say why.

quests.title: Three sweets, lights low and a story that ends well
quests.why: Halloween is a lot of fizz in one night. Your body needs a slow landing.
steps: Choose three sweets for tonight and put the rest away for another day.
Lights low, and a grown-up makes a warm drink.
A story with a happy ending, then bed.

quests.title: Play snap apple: catch a hanging apple with no hands
quests.why: In Ireland, Halloween was once called Snap-Apple Night, after this game.
steps: A grown-up hangs apples on strings from a doorframe or a washing line, at mouth height.
Hands behind your back, try to take a bite with no hands at all.
Take turns, and cheer whoever gets the first bite.

quests.title: Make colcannon, the Irish Halloween mash, with a grown-up
quests.why: In Ireland, colcannon was eaten at Halloween, with little charms hidden inside to tell fortunes. Ours has no charms.
steps: Ask who is eating and about milk allergies. Chop cabbage or kale with the claw, your grown-up beside you.
A grown-up boils the potatoes and softens the greens in a little butter at the hob. You get the masher and the bowls ready.
Mash it all together and serve it with a pool of butter in the middle.

quests.title: Hollow out a turnip lantern, the old way
quests.why: A turnip is far harder than a pumpkin. Scottish guisers carried them anyway, and called them neep lanterns.
steps: A grown-up cuts off the top and carves the face. The knife stays with them.
You hollow it out with a strong metal spoon. It takes a while.
Put a battery tealight inside and set it beside a pumpkin to compare.

quests.title: Make a welcome sign and a no-knocking sign, and offer one to a neighbour
quests.why: A pumpkin in the window says trick-or-treaters are welcome. Some people would rather not have a knock after dark, and a sign lets them say so.
steps: Make two signs: “Trick-or-treaters welcome” and “No knocking tonight, thank you”.
Decide with your grown-up which one your door needs.
With your grown-up, offer the other one to a neighbour you know.

quests.title: Draw the firework code as a poster for your door
quests.why: The firework code: only grown-ups light fireworks, everyone stands well back, and nobody goes back to a lit one.
steps: Ask a grown-up for the three big rules: stand back, never go back, pets indoors.
Draw each rule as a picture.
Stick it up where everyone sees it before 5 November.

quests.title: Build a quiet den for a pet before the bangs start
quests.why: Animals hear fireworks far louder than we do. A dark, hidden den helps them feel safe.
steps: Pick the quietest room with a grown-up.
Make a den with a blanket over a chair or crate, with their bed and a toy inside.
Close the curtains at dusk, then stay calm nearby. No fuss needed.

quests.title: Blow paint through a straw to make firework bursts
quests.why: Firework colours come from metals: copper burns blue, sodium yellow and strontium red.
steps: Drop a blob of runny paint on dark paper.
Blow through a straw to burst it outwards. Blow, never suck.
Add more bursts in new colours, one at a time.

quests.title: Watch the fireworks from a window, warm and cosy
quests.why: People have lit bonfires on 5 November since 1605, the year a plot to blow up Parliament was stopped.
steps: Blanket, a warm drink and the room lights off.
Count the colours you see and name your favourite.
If the bangs feel too loud, ear defenders or hands over your ears are fine.

quests.title: Write your name in sparkler light, done the safe way
quests.why: A sparkler burns many times hotter than an oven, so the rules matter more than the shapes.
steps: Outside only. Gloves on, sleeves down, a bucket of cold water ready.
A grown-up lights one sparkler and hands it to you. Hold it at arm’s length, away from everyone.
Write your name in the air, then put it straight into the water, hot end down.

quests.title: Tell the 1605 Gunpowder Plot story in one minute
quests.why: Guy Fawkes was caught guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder in a cellar under the House of Lords.
steps: Find the story in a book or with a grown-up.
Pick the five facts that matter most.
Tell it to your family in one minute, with a timer running.

quests.title: Bake parkin, the sticky Bonfire Night cake, with a grown-up at the oven
quests.why: In Yorkshire and Lancashire, parkin, a sticky oat and ginger cake, is the Bonfire Night bake.
steps: Ask about allergies first: parkin has oats, flour and butter, and usually egg and milk.
Weigh and mix it yourself. A grown-up warms the butter and syrup, and does the oven.
Leave it a day if you can. Parkin gets stickier as it waits.

quests.title: Make a hedgehog check sign for bonfire builders
quests.why: Hedgehogs look for a dry pile of sticks to sleep in. A bonfire built days early can have one hiding inside.
steps: Find out with a grown-up why hedgehogs crawl into bonfire piles in November.
Make a sign: build it on the day, and check underneath before it’s lit.
With your grown-up, give it to whoever builds a bonfire near you, or put it in your window.

quests.title: Find out the firework rules, and the four nights they change
quests.why: In England and Wales, fireworks can’t be set off between 11pm and 7am, except later on Bonfire Night, New Year’s Eve, Diwali and Lunar New Year.
steps: With a grown-up, find the firework rules for where you live, from a government or council website.
Write down the curfew time, and the four nights it moves.
Add the rule you think matters most for pets and neighbours, and share it at tea.

quests.title: Write your name in torchlight for a long-exposure photo
quests.why: Sparkler names in photos are made with a long exposure: the camera keeps looking while the light moves. A torch works the same way, with no heat.
steps: Lights off, with a torch or a glow stick in your hand.
A grown-up sets a phone camera to night mode or a long exposure and holds it still.
Write your name in the air slowly, then look at the photo together.

quests.title: Draw a rangoli pattern at your front door
quests.why: A rangoli at the door says welcome. At Diwali it welcomes guests, and the goddess Lakshmi, into the home.
steps: Chalk on the doorstep, or coloured rice or paper on a tray by the door.
Start with a dot in the middle and build out in rings: petals, then lamps, then dots.
Keep both sides matching, then show the first person who comes to the door.

quests.title: Make a clay diya and light it with a battery tealight
quests.why: Diwali means ‘rows of lamps’. In the story, lamps lit the way home for Rama and Sita.
steps: Press a ball of air-dry clay into a little pot with a pinched spout.
Leave it to dry overnight, then paint it bright.
Put a battery tealight inside. Never a real flame.

quests.title: Make coconut and cardamom ladoo with a grown-up
quests.why: At Diwali, families make mithai, sweets, and take plates of them round to friends and neighbours.
steps: Mix desiccated coconut, condensed milk and a pinch of ground cardamom with a grown-up.
Roll into small balls with damp hands, then roll them in more coconut.
Ask about allergies, then share some on a plate, the Diwali way.

quests.title: Learn the story of Rama and Sita and tell it in four pictures
quests.why: It’s the story many Hindus remember at Diwali: good beats evil, and light beats darkness.
steps: Read the story with a grown-up, or ask someone who celebrates Diwali to tell it.
Draw four boxes: the forest, Sita taken by Ravana, the battle to rescue her, the lamps.
Tell it back to your family using your four pictures.

quests.title: Find out why Hindus, Sikhs and Jains all light lamps at Diwali
quests.why: Sikhs mark the same night as Bandi Chhor Divas, remembering Guru Hargobind’s release from prison.
steps: Find out what the festival means for Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, with a grown-up.
Write one line for each.
Share them at tea and see who knew all three.

quests.title: Help get the doorway bright and welcoming for Diwali
quests.why: Before Diwali, homes are cleaned and lit up so they feel fresh and welcoming for the new year.
steps: Sweep the doorstep and tidy the hall with a grown-up.
Shake out the mat and line up the shoes.
Put fairy lights or your diya by the door.

quests.title: Make a Diwali card and learn to say Happy Diwali two ways
quests.why: Lots of families send cards and boxes of sweets at Diwali. Shubh Deepavali wishes someone a good and lucky Diwali.
steps: Draw rows of diyas or a rangoli pattern on the front.
Inside, write Happy Diwali, or Shubh Deepavali.
Give it to someone who celebrates, or stand it by your door.

quests.title: Make an akash kandil, a star lantern for the window
quests.why: In Maharashtra, families hang a paper star lantern called an akash kandil, a ‘sky lamp’, outside the home at Diwali.
steps: Draw a big star on card twice and cut both out, a grown-up helping with the points.
Join them with card strips so there is a gap between, and add paper tassels at the bottom.
Hang it in a window with a battery fairy light inside. Never a real flame.

quests.title: Learn the five days of Diwali and mark each one
quests.why: Diwali lasts five days, from Dhanteras to Bhai Dooj, a day for brothers and sisters.
steps: Find the names of the five days with a grown-up.
Draw five boxes and write one thing that happens on each day.
Tick off each day as it comes.

quests.title: Make a paper poppy and learn why it’s red
quests.why: Red poppies grew on the fields where soldiers fought in the First World War, so the poppy became the flower for remembering.
steps: Cut a red paper circle with wavy edges, and a small black circle.
Stick the black one in the middle and add a green paper stem.
Wear it, or put it in a window for Remembrance Sunday.

quests.title: Keep the two-minute silence at eleven o’clock
quests.why: The First World War ended at 11 o’clock on 11 November 1918. Each year people stop for two minutes to remember.
steps: Find out with a grown-up when it is: 11am on 11 November, or on Remembrance Sunday.
Stand or sit still for two minutes. No talking.
Afterwards, say who or what you thought about.

quests.title: Make a purple poppy for the animals who served
quests.why: Horses, dogs and pigeons served in wartime. Some pigeons even won the Dickin Medal, the animals’ medal for bravery.
steps: Find out about one animal that helped: a horse, a messenger pigeon or a dog.
Make a purple poppy from paper or felt.
Tell someone that animal’s story.

quests.title: Find out who served from around the world, not just Britain
quests.why: More than a million soldiers from India served in the First World War, alongside soldiers from Africa and the Caribbean.
steps: With a grown-up, find out which countries soldiers came from.
Find one person’s story, like Khudadad Khan, the first Indian soldier to win the Victoria Cross.
Tell your family one thing you learned.

quests.title: Walk to your local war memorial with a grown-up and read the names
quests.why: Most towns and villages in the UK have a memorial, put up so local names would never be forgotten.
steps: Find your nearest memorial with a grown-up and walk there.
Read some of the names quietly, and look for the dates.
Leave your poppy if you’d like, or just stand for a moment.

quests.title: Make a poppy wreath on a paper plate
quests.why: On Remembrance Sunday, wreaths of poppies are laid at the Cenotaph in London and at memorials all over the UK.
steps: Cut the middle out of a paper plate to make a ring.
Make eight small red poppies from paper circles, each with a black centre.
Stick them round the ring with green leaves between, and hang it in a window.

quests.title: Listen to the Last Post and find out why it’s played
quests.why: The Last Post was a bugle call that marked the end of a soldier’s day. Now it’s played before the two-minute silence.
steps: Find a recording of the Last Post with a grown-up.
Sit still and listen all the way through.
Talk about how it made you feel, and why it might be played on this day.

quests.title: Make a peace dove and write a wish for peace
quests.why: An armistice is an agreement to stop fighting. The one that ended the First World War was signed in a railway carriage in France.
steps: Draw round your hand on white paper: your thumb is the head, your fingers are the wings.
Cut it out and write a wish for peace on it.
Hang it beside your poppy, or in a window.

quests.title: Sow red poppy seeds to flower next summer
quests.why: Poppy seeds can wait in the ground for years and grow when the soil is dug up. That’s why poppies covered the churned-up fields of the First World War.
steps: Get some red field poppy seeds with a grown-up.
Scatter them thinly on bare soil in a pot or a patch of garden, and press them in gently.
Water them, label the spot, and look for flowers next summer.

quests.title: Pick a small challenge and do it on five days
quests.why: Lots of families raise money for children’s charities with a challenge. Grown-ups look after any money.
steps: Pick something you can do each day: 50 star jumps, a lap of the park, 100 skips.
Do it on five days. A grown-up ticks each one off.
Your grown-ups decide about giving, and handle any money.

quests.title: Spotty day: wear spots, then hunt for twenty spotty things
quests.why: Spots are the appeal’s pattern. They’re a reminder that some children need a bit of extra help.
steps: Wear something spotty, or draw spots on a sticker.
Hunt the house for twenty spotty things: dice, dominoes, a ladybird.
Ask a grown-up who the appeal helps, and say it back.

quests.title: Find a project near you that helps children, and what it does
quests.why: The appeal funds youth clubs, family centres, hospices and helplines all over the UK.
steps: With a grown-up, look up a children’s project in your area.
Find three things: who it helps, how, and what it needs.
Tell your family at tea, and decide together if you’d like to help.

quests.title: Bake spotty biscuits for a cake sale, with a label for allergies
quests.why: Cake sales are one of the oldest ways schools raise money for children who need it.
steps: Bake plain biscuits with a grown-up for the oven.
Ice them with spots in as many colours as you can.
Write a label of what’s in them, for anyone with allergies. Grown-ups handle any money.

quests.title: Draw the people who listen to you, help you and believe in you
quests.why: The idea behind the appeal: every child needs someone to listen, someone to help and someone to believe in them.
steps: Draw three circles: listens, helps, believes in me.
Put a name or a drawing of someone in each one.
Show the drawing to one of them.

quests.title: Make spotty bunting for your window
quests.why: The appeal has been on TV every November since 1980, and spots have been its pattern for years.
steps: Cut paper triangles, one for every letter of a word like HELLO or KIND.
Fill each one with spots in different colours and sizes, and add a letter.
Thread them on string and hang them in a window for appeal week.

quests.title: Choose toys or books you’ve outgrown for a children’s charity shop
quests.why: Many children’s charities run shops, where things you no longer need are sold to help children who need it.
steps: Pick toys, books or games you’ve grown out of, clean and with all their pieces.
Check every one with a grown-up before it goes in the bag.
Take it to a children’s charity shop together.

quests.title: Teach a younger child something you’re good at
quests.why: The appeal says every child needs someone to believe in them. Teaching someone younger is one way to be that person.
steps: Pick a younger brother, sister, cousin or family friend, with your grown-up there.
Teach them one thing you can do: a card trick, a paper plane, tying a lace.
Cheer every try, and stop while it’s still fun.

quests.title: Make a spotty stepping-stone path and hop it
quests.why: The appeal funds youth clubs and community groups all over the UK, places where children get to play.
steps: Cut big paper spots and tape them across the floor, a step apart.
Hop from spot to spot to the end without touching the floor.
Move them a little further apart each go, and time your best.

quests.title: Play the listening game: one minute to talk, one minute to listen
quests.why: The appeal’s idea is that every child needs someone to listen. Listening without interrupting takes practice.
steps: Sit with someone at home and set a timer for one minute.
They talk about anything while you just listen. No interrupting.
Tell them the three things you remember, then swap.

quests.title: Odd Socks Day: wear two odd socks and design a third
quests.why: Odd Socks Day starts Anti-Bullying Week. Odd socks say everyone’s different, and that’s fine.
steps: Pick two socks that don’t match.
Design a sock of your own on paper: any pattern, any colour.
Tell someone one thing that makes you a bit different.

quests.title: Name three grown-ups you could tell if something felt wrong
quests.why: This year’s Anti-Bullying Week is about breaking the silence. Knowing who you’d tell makes telling easier.
steps: Draw round your hand.
On three fingers, write a grown-up you could tell: one at home, one at school, one more.
Show your hand to one of them.

quests.title: Learn STOP: what makes something bullying
quests.why: Bullying is hurting someone on purpose, again and again, when it’s hard for them to stop it. Several Times On Purpose.
steps: Learn what STOP stands for with a grown-up.
Talk about the difference between a falling-out and bullying.
Agree what you’d do if you saw it: who you’d tell, and when.

quests.title: Practise three ways to ask someone to join in
quests.why: Being left out hurts, and it’s one of the ways bullying starts. One “want to join in?” can stop it.
steps: Think of three ways to invite someone: a game, a seat, a team.
Practise each one out loud with a grown-up.
Use one this week, at school or at the park.

quests.title: Plan what you’d do if a group chat turned on someone
quests.why: Bullying usually has people watching. One watcher who acts, or tells, can change it.
steps: Picture it: a chat where everyone’s laughing at one person.
Write three things you could do: message them kindly, save the messages, tell a grown-up.
Talk your list through with a grown-up you trust.

quests.title: Make a worry post box for your home
quests.why: Some things are hard to say out loud. Writing them down is another way to break the silence.
steps: Decorate a box and cut a slot in the lid.
Agree with your grown-ups when they’ll check it, and that it stays private.
Post one note to test it, even a small one.

quests.title: Make a kind-words paper chain for your home
quests.why: This year’s theme, Break the Silence, was shaped by more than 200 children. Kind words are an easy way to start a conversation.
steps: Cut paper strips, one for everyone at home and a few spare.
On each, write something kind and true about that person.
Loop them into a chain and hang it where everyone can read it.

quests.title: Practise how to tell: what happened, where and who
quests.why: Telling isn’t telling tales. Telling tales gets someone into trouble. Telling a grown-up gets someone out of it.
steps: With a grown-up, make up a small pretend problem, like a lost pencil case.
Practise telling it: what happened, where, when and who was there.
Agree together what your grown-up will do when you tell them something real.

quests.title: Play “how do they feel?” and notice who’s gone quiet
quests.why: Break the Silence is about noticing when someone has gone quiet, then doing something kind about it.
steps: Take turns to show a feeling with your face and body, no words: proud, left out, worried, excited.
Guess each other’s, and say what gave it away.
Talk about how you’d spot someone at school who looks left out, and one thing you’d do.

quests.title: Make a card dreidel, learn its four letters and play
quests.why: The four Hebrew letters on a dreidel stand for ‘a great miracle happened there’.
steps: Fold a card net into a cube and push a pencil through the middle.
Write nun, gimel, hey and shin on the sides. Nun: nothing. Gimel: take all. Hey: take half. Shin: put one in.
Everyone puts in a raisin or a button, then take turns to spin.

quests.title: Make a paper menorah and add a flame each night of Hanukkah
quests.why: A Hanukkah menorah has nine branches: one for each of the eight nights, and a helper candle, the shamash, that lights the rest.
steps: Draw or cut out a menorah with nine candles, the middle one taller.
Stick it in a window, where Hanukkah lights are meant to be seen.
Night one: a flame for the shamash and one for the first candle. Then add one more paper flame each night.

quests.title: Make potato latkes with a grown-up
quests.why: Hanukkah foods are fried in oil, to remember the oil that lasted eight nights.
steps: Grate potato and onion with a grown-up, minding your knuckles, then squeeze out the water in a clean tea towel.
Mix in an egg, a spoon of flour and a pinch of salt.
A grown-up fries them in hot oil. You serve them with apple sauce or soured cream.

quests.title: Learn the Hanukkah story and tell it in eight pictures
quests.why: Hanukkah means ‘dedication’. It remembers the Temple in Jerusalem being made ready again, more than 2,000 years ago.
steps: Read the story with a grown-up, or ask someone who celebrates to share it.
Draw it in eight small boxes, one for each night.
Tell it back using your pictures.

quests.title: Learn to say Chag Sameach and make a Hanukkah card
quests.why: Chag Sameach means ‘happy festival’ in Hebrew. Happy Hanukkah is right too.
steps: Make a card with a menorah, a dreidel or a doughnut on the front.
Write Happy Hanukkah or Chag Sameach inside.
Give it to someone who celebrates, or put it in your window.

quests.title: Fill doughnuts with jam, like sufganiyot
quests.why: In Israel, sufganiyot, jam doughnuts, are the Hanukkah treat. Like latkes, they’re fried in oil.
steps: Ask about allergies first: doughnuts have gluten, egg and milk.
Take plain shop doughnuts and make a small hole in the side of each with a chopstick.
Pipe or spoon in some jam, dust with icing sugar and share them on a plate.

quests.title: Work out how many candles all eight nights of Hanukkah need
quests.why: A box of Hanukkah candles holds 44: one more each night, plus the shamash every night.
steps: Line up buttons or blocks: one for night one, two for night two, all the way to eight.
Add one more to every night for the shamash, the helper candle.
Count them all, then check a real box of Hanukkah candles if someone has one.

quests.title: Make an oil and water jar, and see why oil floats
quests.why: The Hanukkah story is about a little jar of oil that was enough for one night and lasted eight.
steps: Fill a clear plastic bottle a quarter full of water and add a drop of food colouring.
Top it up with cooking oil, a grown-up holding the bottle, and watch the oil float on top.
Lid on tight, tip it slowly, and shine a torch through it.

quests.title: Make a paper chain that counts down the days to Christmas
quests.why: Advent means ‘arrival’: the weeks when Christians get ready for Christmas.
steps: Count the days left until 25 December, and cut a paper strip for each one.
Loop them into a chain with glue or tape, and hang it up.
Each morning, tear one link off and count how many are left.

quests.title: Hear the Christmas story and tell it in four pictures
quests.why: Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus at Christmas. The story says he was born in a stable in Bethlehem because there was no room at the inn.
steps: Read the Christmas story with a grown-up, from a children’s book.
Draw four boxes: a long journey, a full inn, a stable, a bright star.
Tell the story back to your family using your four pictures.

quests.title: Make a thank-you card for someone who works on Christmas Day
quests.why: Nurses, carers, paramedics and many others work on 25 December, so everyone else is safe and looked after.
steps: Think of someone who works on Christmas Day: a nurse, a carer, a paramedic, a bus driver.
Make a card that says thank you, and exactly what for.
Give it with a grown-up, or post it together to a hospital or care home near you.

quests.title: Make a Christingle and find out what each part means
quests.why: A Christingle is an orange for the world with a light on top. Moravian Christians in Germany made the first ones in 1747.
steps: Tie a red ribbon or a strip of red tape round the middle of an orange.
Push in four cocktail sticks, each with a few raisins or sweets on the end.
A grown-up makes a small hole in the top for a battery tealight. Never a real flame.

quests.title: Learn a carol and find out where it comes from
quests.why: ‘Silent Night’ was first sung on Christmas Eve 1818 in a village church in Austria, to a guitar.
steps: Pick a carol with a grown-up and listen to it together.
Learn the first verse, a line at a time.
Sing it to your family, and tell them one thing about where it comes from.

quests.title: Find out how the Christmas tree came to Britain
quests.why: Queen Charlotte, who grew up in Germany, put up one of the first Christmas trees in England in 1800. A picture of Queen Victoria’s family round theirs in 1848 made them popular.
steps: Find out with a grown-up where the Christmas tree custom began, and how it reached Britain.
Draw a tree and write three facts round it.
Share your facts at tea, and ask who had a tree when they were small.

quests.title: Make a Christmas cracker with your own joke inside
quests.why: A London sweet maker, Tom Smith, made the first Christmas crackers in 1847, after seeing sweets wrapped in twists of paper in Paris.
steps: Wrap a toilet roll tube in paper, leaving extra paper at each end.
Put inside a paper hat you made and a joke you wrote yourself.
Twist the ends, tie them with ribbon, and pull it with someone at the table.

quests.title: Fill a Boxing Day box for people who need it
quests.why: Boxing Day, 26 December, may take its name from the Christmas boxes once given to people who worked for others, and to the poor.
steps: With a grown-up, choose tins and packets from the cupboard that your family can spare.
Check the dates, then pack them in a box with a kind note on top.
Take it to a food bank or a collection point together.

quests.title: Go on a lights walk after dark and count the stars in windows
quests.why: Stars go up at Christmas because the story tells of a bright star that led wise men to Bethlehem.
steps: Wrap up warm and go for a walk after dark with a grown-up.
Count every star you see in windows, on doors and on houses.
Pick your favourite, and draw it when you get home.

quests.title: Make mince pies, with a grown-up at the oven
quests.why: Mince pies once had real minced meat in them. Today’s mincemeat is mostly dried fruit, apple and spice.
steps: Ask who is eating first: pastry has wheat and butter, and mincemeat can have nuts or suet in it.
Press pastry circles into a bun tray, add a spoon of mincemeat and put a pastry star on top.
A grown-up bakes them in the oven. Let them cool, then share a plate.

quests.title: Find out how Christmas is kept in three countries
quests.why: In Ethiopia, Christmas is called Genna and falls on 7 January, as it does for many Orthodox Christians.
steps: With a grown-up, pick three countries on three different continents.
For each, find one Christmas food, one custom and the date it’s kept.
Make a little table and share it at tea.

quests.title: Make a quiet spot for when Christmas gets too busy
quests.why: Lots of people find the days around Christmas noisy and busy. Ten quiet minutes somewhere calm helps anyone feel steady again.
steps: Pick a calm corner and give it a blanket, a cushion, a book and something soft.
Tell everyone at home it’s there, and that anyone can use it.
On the busiest day, go there for ten quiet minutes whenever you need to.

quests.title: Make a family time capsule to open next New Year
quests.why: A time capsule is a message to the future. Some wait a hundred years. Yours only has to wait one.
steps: Find a box or a jar with a lid.
Ask everyone at home for one thing: a drawing, a note, a ticket or a guess about the year ahead.
Close it up, write the day to open it on the lid, and hide it somewhere safe.

quests.title: Make a page of three things you’re proud of from the year just gone
quests.why: Looking back at what went well helps you see how much you’ve grown, even in a year that felt hard.
steps: Think back through the year: school, home, friends and things you tried.
Pick three things you’re proud of, big or small.
Draw or write them on one page, and keep it where you’ll see it.

quests.title: Choose one goal for the year and plan its first three steps
quests.why: Big goals are easier as a few steps. Planning when you’ll take the first one makes it far more likely to happen.
steps: Pick one thing you’d like to be able to do by next New Year.
Write three steps towards it, and the day you’ll take the first one.
Tell someone at home, so they can ask how it’s going.

quests.title: Pick one new thing to learn this year, and draw yourself doing it
quests.why: A new year is a good time to start something. Drawing it helps you remember what you’re aiming for.
steps: Think of one thing you’d love to learn: to whistle, to ride a bike or to tie your laces.
Draw a picture of you doing it.
Stick it on the fridge and tell a grown-up your very first step.

quests.title: Count down to midnight somewhere else, at a time your grown-up picks
quests.why: New Year arrives one time zone at a time. It starts in the Pacific and takes about 26 hours to reach everywhere.
steps: Your grown-ups pick when your family counts down: real midnight, or an earlier one.
Find a country where it’s midnight at that time, and find it on a map or a globe.
Count down from ten together and cheer in their new year.

quests.title: Be your home’s first-footer, the way Hogmanay is kept in Scotland
quests.why: In Scotland, New Year’s Eve is Hogmanay. The first person over the doorstep in the new year, the first-footer, brings gifts for luck.
steps: Find out with a grown-up what a first-footer carries: often shortbread, salt and coal, for food, flavour and warmth.
Pack a little bag of luck gifts from home: a biscuit, a pinch of salt in paper and something warm, like socks.
On New Year’s Day, be first in through your own front door and hand them out.

quests.title: Write a letter to yourself to open next New Year
quests.why: In a year you’ll have grown, learned loads and changed your mind about things. A letter lets you see how much.
steps: Write to yourself a year from now: your best friend, your favourite food, what you’re into right now.
Fold it into an envelope and write the day to open it on the front.
Put it in your family time capsule, or somewhere safe.

quests.title: Write a wish for each person at home and read them out on New Year’s Day
quests.why: In Japan, people send nengajō, New Year cards wishing friends and family a good year, timed to arrive on 1 January.
steps: Cut a slip of paper for each person at home.
On each, write one thing you hope goes well for them this year.
Fold them into a jar and read them out together on New Year’s Day.

quests.title: Make up a twelve-move dance, one move for each month, and teach it
quests.why: At Hogmanay, people in Scotland link arms for ‘Auld Lang Syne’, a song Robert Burns wrote down in 1788.
steps: Make up a dance with twelve moves, one for each month of the new year.
Teach it to someone at home.
Dance it together on New Year’s Eve or New Year’s Day, to a song you all like.

quests.title: Plan a New Year’s Eve the whole family agrees on
quests.why: Families keep New Year in very different ways, and plenty sleep right through it. The best plan is the one everyone agrees to.
steps: Ask everyone at home what they’d like: an early countdown, a film, games or bed at the usual time.
Agree the plan with your grown-ups, including when the youngest go to bed.
Run it on the night: set out the games, keep an eye on the time and start the countdown.

quests.title: Find out why the year starts in January, and the other new years people keep
quests.why: January is named after Janus, the Roman god with two faces: one looking back, one looking forward.
steps: Find out with a grown-up why January is the first month, and where its name comes from.
Find two other new years kept in Britain, like Lunar New Year, Rosh Hashanah or Vaisakhi.
Draw Janus looking both ways: last year on one side, this year on the other.

quests.title: Make a shaker to welcome the new year
