quests.why: People have made a happy noise at New Year for hundreds of years, with bells, pans and cheers.
steps: Put a spoon of rice or dried beans in a small clean bottle or tub.
A grown-up tapes the lid on tight.
Decorate it, then shake it at your countdown.

quests.title: Make a red paper lantern for the Lantern Festival
quests.why: New Year celebrations end on the fifteenth day with the Lantern Festival, under the first full moon.
steps: Fold a sheet of red paper in half the long way.
With safe scissors, cut slits from the fold, stopping short of the edge.
Open it, roll it into a tube, glue it, add a handle and hang it in a window.

quests.title: Find your zodiac animal and hear the story of the Great Race
quests.why: Twelve animals raced across a river to name the years. 2027 is the Year of the Goat.
steps: Hear or read the story of the Great Race.
Find the animal for each person at home. Born in January or early February? The animal changes at Lunar New Year, so check the date.
Draw everyone’s animals in the order they finished.

quests.title: Sweep out the old year, then hide the broom
quests.why: Families clean before the new year to sweep out bad luck, then put the broom away so the good luck stays.
steps: Pick one room to sweep or hoover with a grown-up, the day before.
Get every corner. You’re clearing out the old year.
Put the broom away. No sweeping on New Year’s Day.

quests.title: Write a good-luck wish in red for everyone at home
quests.why: Red means luck at New Year. Some families hang the character for luck, fu, upside down, because ‘upside down’ sounds like ‘luck arrives’.
steps: Cut red paper into diamonds, one for each person at home.
Write or draw a wish on each: good health, lots of laughs, a happy year.
Hand them out and say “Xin nian kuai le”, Happy New Year in Mandarin.

quests.title: Fold dumplings for the New Year’s Eve meal with a grown-up
quests.why: In northern China, dumplings are folded to look like old gold ingots, for a lucky year ahead.
steps: Mix a filling your family eats with a grown-up: vegetables, tofu, chicken or pork.
A spoonful in the middle of each wrapper, wet the edge, fold and pinch.
A grown-up cooks them. Count how many you folded.

quests.title: Make a lion dance head from a box and dance to a drumbeat
quests.why: Lion dancers leap to drums and cymbals at New Year to chase off bad luck and welcome good luck in.
steps: Turn a cardboard box into a lion head: big eyes, a red and gold mane.
Someone beats a pan like a drum: boom, boom, crash.
Dance the lion round every room, and leap on every crash.

quests.title: Learn to say Happy New Year in Mandarin, Vietnamese and Korean
quests.why: Lunar New Year is Tết in Vietnam and Seollal in Korea, as well as the Spring Festival in China.
steps: With a grown-up, learn Xin nian kuai le (Mandarin), Chúc mừng năm mới (Vietnamese) and Saehae bok mani badeuseyo (Korean).
Practise each one until you can say it without looking.
Say all three at tea, and see who can say them back.

quests.title: Make lolly-stick yut and play yut nori, the Korean New Year game
quests.why: In Korea, families play yut nori at Seollal, throwing four sticks to see how far to move.
steps: Colour one side of four lolly sticks, and draw a board: a square of dots with a cross through the middle.
Throw the sticks and move one dot for each coloured side that lands up. None up means five.
Race two counters each all the way round, taking the shortcuts across the middle.

quests.title: Build a book character from things already at home
quests.why: World Book Day is about reading for fun. A costume from the dressing-up box counts, and so do pyjamas.
steps: Pick a character from a book you’ve read.
Find three things at home that say who they are: a hat, a scarf, a prop.
Say one line they’d say, and see who guesses.

quests.title: Read by torchlight in a blanket den
quests.why: World Book Day in the UK and Ireland began in 1997. It’s about reading for fun, nothing else.
steps: Make a quick blanket den and grab a torch.
Pick any book, comic or magazine. It all counts.
Twenty minutes, then tell someone your favourite bit.

quests.title: Swap a book you loved, with a note inside
quests.why: A book you loved can be someone else’s new favourite. Swapping is how stories travel.
steps: Pick a book you loved and have finished.
Write a note for inside the cover: why it’s good, no spoilers.
Swap it with someone at home, a friend or a cousin.

quests.title: Fold one sheet into an eight-page mini book and write a story in it
quests.why: Every book in the library started as someone’s first draft. On World Book Day, yours counts too.
steps: Fold and cut one sheet of paper into an eight-page mini book.
A cover, a title page, then a story across six pages.
Read it aloud to someone at home.

quests.title: Visit the library and pick a book you’d normally walk past
quests.why: UK public libraries are free to join, at any age.
steps: Go with a grown-up, and join if you haven’t already.
Pick one book you’d never normally choose.
Read the first chapter, or first five pages, by the weekend.

quests.title: Act out a story while someone reads it, every action word
quests.why: World Book Day is held in more than 100 countries. The UK and Ireland keep it in March, so it doesn’t fall in the Easter holidays.
steps: Pick a story full of action: a chase, a storm, a hunt.
Someone reads it aloud while you act out every action word.
Swap, so you read while they act.

quests.title: Start a family book club: one story, everyone reads it
quests.why: World Book Day turns 30 in 2027. It started in the UK and Ireland in 1997.
steps: Choose one short book or story that everyone at home can read or hear.
Give everyone a week to read it, or read it aloud together.
Meet at tea: favourite bit, least favourite bit, and a score out of ten.

quests.title: Read aloud to someone younger, a pet or a row of toys
quests.why: Some UK libraries run sessions where children read to calm dogs. A listener who never corrects you makes reading aloud easier.
steps: Pick a book you can read, or a picture book you know well.
Read it aloud to a younger child, a pet or your toys. Do the voices.
Stop at the exciting bit and ask your listener what happens next.

quests.title: Help lay an iftar table: dates, water and something to share
quests.why: In Ramadan many Muslims fast from dawn to sunset, then open the fast with a date and water. Anyone can share the meal.
steps: Ask a grown-up what time sunset is today.
Set out dates, water and a dish for everyone.
Have the table ready for the moment the sun sets.

quests.title: Make crescent moons and stars for the window for Eid
quests.why: Eid begins when the new crescent moon is seen, so its date can move by a day.
steps: Draw and cut out a crescent moon and some stars.
Add gold pen or glitter, and a hole for string.
Hang them in a window the night before Eid.

quests.title: Moon watch: look for the thin new moon after sunset
quests.why: The Islamic calendar follows the moon. A new month, and Eid, begins when the first thin crescent is seen.
steps: With a grown-up, find out when sunset is and which way is west.
Just after sunset, look low in the western sky together.
Draw what you see each evening, even if it’s only cloud.

quests.title: Pack a food gift before Eid, so another family can celebrate
quests.why: Before Eid prayers, Muslims give food or money, called zakat al-fitr, so every family can celebrate.
steps: Ask a grown-up what your local food bank needs most.
Choose and pack the food together. Check the dates.
Drop it off together before Eid.

quests.title: Learn what Eid Mubarak means and say it to someone
quests.why: Eid Mubarak means ‘blessed celebration’. Eid al-Fitr marks the end of a month of fasting.
steps: Learn Ramadan Mubarak for the month, and Eid Mubarak for the day.
Find out one way your friends or neighbours celebrate Eid.
Say it to someone who celebrates, or write it in a card.

quests.title: Make sheer khurma, an Eid morning pudding, with a grown-up
quests.why: Sheer khurma means ‘milk with dates’. Many South Asian Muslim families eat it on Eid morning.
steps: Ask about allergies first: it has milk and wheat, and often nuts. A grown-up toasts thin vermicelli in a little butter or ghee at the hob.
Measure the milk, chop soft dates with a table knife and add a pinch of cardamom. A grown-up stirs it on the hob as it thickens.
Serve it warm in small bowls. Leave the nuts off if anyone has an allergy.

quests.title: Make a fanous, a Ramadan lantern, with a battery light
quests.why: In Egypt, children carry a fanous, a bright lantern, through the streets in Ramadan.
steps: Fold card into a tall box with windows, cut out by you and a grown-up.
Cover the windows with coloured tissue paper and add a handle.
Put a battery tealight inside. Never a real flame.

quests.title: Make a small Eid treat bag for someone who celebrates
quests.why: On Eid, children are often given small gifts, and families share sweet dishes with friends and neighbours.
steps: Decorate a paper bag with a crescent moon and stars.
Ask about allergies, then fill it with dates or sweets. Check the sweets are halal: many jelly sweets have pork gelatine.
Give it with a grown-up, and say Eid Mubarak.

quests.title: Make fruit chaat for an iftar table, with a grown-up
quests.why: Fruit chaat, chopped fruit with lemon and a pinch of spicy chaat masala, is on many South Asian iftar tables.
steps: Ask who is eating and about allergies, then wash the fruit: apple, banana, grapes, melon.
Chop it with the claw, your grown-up beside you.
Add a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chaat masala, and have it ready for sunset.

quests.title: Serve tea langar-style: everyone sits together as equals
quests.why: At a gurdwara’s langar, anyone can eat for free, side by side, whoever they are. Guru Nanak began it.
steps: Help a grown-up make a simple vegetarian tea: dal and rice, or roti. A grown-up does the hob.
Everyone sits together at the same level, even on a sheet on the floor.
You serve everyone first, and eat last.

quests.title: Learn three bhangra moves and dance the harvest in
quests.why: Bhangra began with Punjabi farmers dancing to the dhol drum to celebrate the wheat harvest at Vaisakhi.
steps: Arms up, shoulders bouncing to the beat.
Hop on one foot while the other kicks forward, then swap.
Find bhangra music with a grown-up and dance to one whole song.

quests.title: Learn the story of the Khalsa and the Panj Pyare
quests.why: At Vaisakhi in 1699, Guru Gobind Singh began the Khalsa. The first five to step forward are called the Panj Pyare, the Five Beloved Ones.
steps: Read the story with a grown-up, or ask someone who is Sikh to share it.
Find out the five Ks and what each one means.
Tell your family one thing that surprised you.

quests.title: Make a Vaisakhi card with a golden harvest picture
quests.why: Vaisakhi is the Sikh new year and the Punjab wheat harvest. People wish each other ‘lakh lakh vadhaiyan’, a hundred thousand congratulations.
steps: Draw golden wheat under a bright sun.
Write Happy Vaisakhi inside.
Give it to someone, or stand it up at home.

quests.title: Do seva: a job for other people, for nothing back
quests.why: Seva means selfless service. At Vaisakhi, Sikhs give their time to cook, clean and serve others.
steps: Pick a job that helps more people than you: the shared bins, a neighbour’s path, washing up for everyone.
Do it with a grown-up, all the way through.
Don’t ask for thanks. That’s the point of seva.

quests.title: Make a box dhol and drum the bhangra beat
quests.why: The dhol is a big drum with two sides: a deep boom on one and a high tap on the other. It drives every bhangra song.
steps: Turn a round tub or a box on its side, so you can play both ends.
Use a wooden spoon on one end for the boom and a pencil on the other for the tap.
Play boom, tap-tap, boom, tap along to bhangra music with a grown-up.

quests.title: Make roti dough from the wheat harvest, and a grown-up cooks them
quests.why: Vaisakhi is the Punjab wheat harvest, and wheat becomes roti, the flatbread at almost every Punjabi meal.
steps: Ask about gluten allergies, then mix wholemeal flour and water and knead it into a soft dough.
Roll small balls into flat circles with a rolling pin.
A grown-up cooks them on a hot pan while you watch them puff up.

quests.title: Find out what happens at a Nagar Kirtan
quests.why: Nagar Kirtan processions in Southall, Birmingham and Leicester are some of the biggest in Europe, and anyone is welcome to watch.
steps: With a grown-up, find pictures or a film of a Nagar Kirtan and what happens in it.
Find out how visitors show respect: a scarf over your head, and a thank you for any food offered.
If there’s one near you, decide with your grown-up whether to go and watch together.

quests.title: Draw a phulkari pattern, the flower work of Punjab
quests.why: Phulkari means ‘flower work’: bright embroidery from Punjab, stitched in golden yellow, red, orange and pink thread.
steps: Look at phulkari pictures with a grown-up and spot the shapes: diamonds, flowers, zigzags.
On dark paper, draw a square with a repeating pattern in bright yellow, orange and pink.
Keep it matching from the middle out, and stand it up with your Vaisakhi card.

quests.title: Grow cress on a windowsill and eat it in a sandwich
quests.why: This Earth Day is about food. Food you grow yourself travels about a metre to your plate.
steps: Put damp kitchen roll or soil in a pot or an empty eggshell.
Sprinkle on cress seeds and put it on a sunny windowsill.
Water a little each day, then eat it in a sandwich in a week.

quests.title: Fridge rescue: find food near its date and plan to eat it first
quests.why: ‘Use by’ is about safety. ‘Best before’ is about taste. Knowing the difference saves food from the bin.
steps: With a grown-up, check the dates on the fridge food.
Move anything close to its date to the front.
Plan one meal or snack that uses it up.

quests.title: Earth Day litter pick: count how much was food packaging
quests.why: A lot of street litter starts life as a snack. Counting it shows you where it comes from.
steps: Gloves on, a bag, a grown-up beside you. A litter picker if you have one.
Pick for twenty minutes. Leave anything sharp or glass for your grown-up.
Count how many pieces were food or drink packaging.

quests.title: Make wildflower seed balls for the bees
quests.why: Bees and other pollinators help grow about one in every three mouthfuls of our food.
steps: Mix compost, a little clay or flour paste and native wildflower seeds.
Roll balls the size of a marble and let them dry.
Plant them in your garden, a pot, or a spot a grown-up says is allowed.

quests.title: Plan a family tea around three vegetables in season in April
quests.why: Food grown nearby and in season usually needs less heating, storing and shipping to reach you.
steps: Find three UK vegetables in season in April: try spring greens, radishes or purple sprouting broccoli.
Plan a tea that uses all three, with a grown-up.
Help get it ready, and tell everyone where the vegetables came from. A grown-up does the hob and the oven.

quests.title: Regrow spring onions from their roots in a glass of water
quests.why: Some food grows back from its scraps. The root end of a spring onion sprouts new green shoots in about a week.
steps: Save the white root ends when spring onions are used, about a thumb long.
Stand them roots down in a glass with a little water, on a windowsill.
Change the water every two days, then snip the new green shoots into a meal.

quests.title: Food miles hunt: find where your fruit and veg were grown
quests.why: Fresh fruit and veg in UK shops must be labelled with the country it was grown in.
steps: Find the labels on the fruit and veg at home, with a grown-up.
Write down each country, and find it on a map or a globe.
Circle the ones grown in the UK, and the one that travelled furthest.

quests.title: Start a peelings tub for compost or the food caddy
quests.why: Peelings in a compost heap turn into food for soil. Buried in landfill, they rot without air and give off methane, a gas that warms the planet.
steps: Find a tub with a lid for the kitchen, with a grown-up.
Fill it with fruit and veg peelings, cores and eggshells after meals.
Empty it into a compost bin or your council food caddy, and keep it going for a week.

quests.title: Ten-minute bee count: watch one patch of flowers and tally the visitors
quests.why: UK scientists ask families to do exactly this: count the insects on a patch of flowers for ten minutes, to see how pollinators are doing.
steps: With a grown-up, find a patch of flowers in a garden, a park or a pot. Sunshine helps.
For ten minutes, tally every insect that lands: bees, hoverflies, butterflies, beetles. Watch, never touch.
Count them up and see which kind visited most.

quests.title: Ask everyone at home how they feel, as a weather
quests.why: Everyone has mental health, the way everyone has a body. This week is for talking about it.
steps: At tea, ask each person to pick a weather for how they feel: sunny, cloudy, windy, rainy or stormy.
Say your own weather too.
Ask one person what would help their weather, and listen.

quests.title: Try the five ways to feel good, one a day for five days
quests.why: Connect, move, notice, learn, give: five small things the NHS says help people feel good.
steps: Day one, talk to someone properly. Day two, move for twenty minutes.
Day three, notice five things outside. Day four, learn one new thing.
Day five, do something kind. Tick each day off.

quests.title: Make a calm jar and watch the glitter settle
quests.why: Shaken glitter is like a busy head. Watch it settle, and your breathing slows down with it.
steps: Fill a plastic jar with warm water, a squeeze of glue and some glitter. A grown-up seals the lid tight.
Give it a big shake.
Breathe slowly while it settles, and time how long it takes.

quests.title: Make a “what helps me” card and show it to a grown-up
quests.why: Knowing what helps you is half the job. Telling someone means they can help too.
steps: Write or draw five things that help on a hard day: a person, a place, a song, a snack, a game.
Keep the card somewhere you can find it.
Show it to a grown-up so they know too.

quests.title: Find three places a young person can go for help, and keep them
quests.why: Childline is free on 0800 1111, day and night. Knowing that before you need it makes it easier.
steps: With a grown-up, look up Childline, Shout and YoungMinds.
Write down what each one does and how to reach it.
Keep the list somewhere private, for you or a friend.

quests.title: Weather before, weather after: a walk that moves your mood
quests.why: Being active is one of the NHS’s five steps to mental wellbeing. A short walk counts.
steps: Before you go, pick a weather for how you feel: sunny, cloudy, windy, rainy or stormy.
Go for a brisk fifteen-minute walk with a grown-up.
Pick your weather again when you get back, and say what changed.

quests.title: Make a jar of talking questions for tea
quests.why: Connecting with other people is the first of the NHS’s five steps to mental wellbeing.
steps: Write ten questions on slips of paper: what made you laugh today, what would you invent, where would you go.
Fold them into a jar.
At tea, everyone pulls one out and answers it.

quests.title: Cloud watching: five minutes of just noticing
quests.why: Paying attention to the present moment is one of the NHS’s five steps to mental wellbeing. Clouds are an easy place to start.
steps: Lie on a blanket outside, or sit by a window, with a grown-up nearby.
Watch the clouds for five minutes. Notice their shapes, speed and colours.
Draw the best shape you saw.

quests.title: Learn one small new thing this week and show someone
quests.why: Mental Health Awareness Week has run since 2001. Learning something new is one of the NHS’s five steps to feeling good.
steps: Pick something small: a card trick, a knot, three words in another language, a new recipe.
Practise it a little each day this week.
Show someone at home what you learned, and how you learned it.

quests.title: Learn the beach safety code before your first water day
quests.why: Knowing the flags means you know where it’s safe to splash.
steps: With a grown-up, find out what the red and yellow flags mean, and what a plain red flag means.
Learn Float to Live: lean back, ears in the water, arms and legs out wide.
Say what to do if someone is in trouble in the water: tell a lifeguard or a grown-up, or call 999 and ask for the Coastguard. Never go in after them.

quests.title: Go rock pooling and spot five different creatures
quests.why: A rock pool is a tiny sea the tide left behind.
steps: Check the tide times, then go at low tide with a grown-up, who stays close.
Walk on sand and bare rock, never the slippery weed.
Spot five different creatures. Look closely, and leave each one where it was.

quests.title: Rescue the toys frozen in a block of ice
quests.why: Ice melts slowly. Unless you help it.
steps: A grown-up freezes small toys in a tub of water overnight.
Tip the ice block onto a tray, outside or in the sink.
Free every toy with warm water, salt and a spoon.

quests.title: Plan the family’s water day: the place, the tide and the kit
quests.why: A good water day is mostly decided before anyone gets wet.
steps: With a grown-up, pick a beach with lifeguards, a lido or a pool.
Check the tide times or the opening times, and the weather.
Write the kit list: sun cream, hats, water, shade and a towel each.

quests.title: Swim further than you could at the start of the summer
quests.why: Swimming gets stronger quietly. Measure it and you’ll see.
steps: Go to a pool with lifeguards, with a grown-up there.
Swim as far as you can without stopping, and write the number down.
Another day this summer, go again and beat it.

quests.title: Go on a minibeast safari and draw your three best finds
quests.why: The garden is full of tiny animals. Most of them are hiding.
steps: Gently lift a log or a stone, then put it back just as it was.
Look under leaves, in long grass and along the bottom of walls.
Draw your three best finds and give each one a name.

quests.title: Sit still in the sun for fifteen minutes and count every butterfly
quests.why: Counting butterflies tells scientists how the summer is going.
steps: Pick a sunny spot in a garden or a park, with a grown-up.
Sit still for fifteen minutes and count every butterfly you see.
Write down your total. A grown-up can send it to the Big Butterfly Count if they like.

quests.title: Set a footprint trap overnight and find out who visited
quests.why: Lots of animals come out at night. They leave clues.
steps: Fill a tray with damp sand or soil and smooth it flat.
Put it outside before bed, with a little dish of water beside it.
In the morning, draw the prints and work out who left them.

quests.title: Go pond dipping and find out what lives under the water
quests.why: A pond looks still on top. Underneath, it’s busy.
steps: Go with a grown-up, who stays right beside you. Kneel on the bank.
Sweep a net slowly through the water and tip it into a tray of pond water.
Name or draw three creatures, then pour them gently back and wash your hands.

quests.title: Build a wildlife hide together and watch quietly for twenty minutes
quests.why: Animals come closer when they can’t see you.
steps: Hang a blanket over chairs or a washing line, near where birds or squirrels come.
Get in together with a notebook. Whispers only.
Twenty minutes. Write or draw every visitor.

quests.title: Make a bee bath so thirsty bees can drink
quests.why: Bees get thirsty on hot days, and they can’t swim.
steps: Find a shallow dish and some pebbles.
Add water until the pebbles just poke out, so bees can land.
Put it near flowers. Top it up on hot days.

quests.title: Stay up with a grown-up to watch for shooting stars
quests.why: Around 12 August the Earth passes through a trail of comet dust, and the sky lights up.
steps: Pick a clear night near 12 August, away from bright lights, with a grown-up.
Lie back on a blanket and give your eyes twenty minutes to get used to the dark.
Count the shooting stars. Make a wish on the best one.

quests.title: Turn a big cardboard box into something you can sit inside
quests.why: A box can be a car, a rocket or a boat. You decide.
steps: Find the biggest box you can. A grown-up cuts any doors or windows.
Decide what it is, then paint it, draw on it and add the details.
Climb in and take it somewhere imaginary.

quests.title: Make a sundial and tell the time by its shadow
quests.why: People told the time by the sun for thousands of years.
steps: Push a stick upright into the ground or a pot, somewhere sunny all day.
Every hour, put a pebble where the shadow ends and write the time on it.
Next sunny day, read the time from the shadow, then check a clock.

quests.title: Build a pizza-box sun oven and melt chocolate on a hot day
quests.why: The sun is a free oven, if you can catch its heat.
steps: A grown-up cuts a flap in the lid of a pizza box. Cover the flap in foil.
Tape cling film over the hole and put black paper in the bottom.
Put chocolate on a biscuit inside, point the flap at the sun and wait.

quests.title: Make a giant bubble wand and blow the biggest bubble you can
quests.why: Big bubbles need slow hands and a still day.
steps: Tie string between two sticks to make a loop.
Mix water, washing-up liquid and a spoon of sugar in a tray.
Dip, lift and walk backwards slowly.

quests.title: Build a cardboard city over three days, adding more each day
quests.why: A city gets built one street at a time.
steps: Day one: boxes and tubes for the buildings, and the streets drawn on a big sheet.
Day two: add roads, a park, a river or a bridge.
Day three: give it a name, some people and a map for visitors.

quests.title: Spaghetti tower: whose stands tallest
quests.why: Triangles make towers strong. Find out who works that out first.
steps: The same kit each: twenty sticks of dry spaghetti and some marshmallows.
Fifteen minutes to build the tallest tower that stands on its own.
A grown-up measures. It has to stand for a whole minute to count.

quests.title: Turn an old T-shirt into a bag, with no sewing
quests.why: An old T-shirt can carry your things for years.
steps: Pick a T-shirt nobody wants, and check with a grown-up.
Cut off the sleeves and the neck, then cut a fringe along the bottom.
Tie the fringe in knots to close the bottom. Fill it and test it.

quests.title: Go berry picking at a farm or a hedge, with a grown-up
quests.why: Berries you picked yourself taste the best.
steps: Go with a grown-up to a pick-your-own farm, or a hedge they know.
Only pick what your grown-up says is safe, and from higher than a dog can reach.
Wash them at home, then share them or bake them into something.

quests.title: Grow a pot of salad leaves and eat them before the summer ends
quests.why: Salad leaves grow fast. Sow them now and eat them in about a month.
steps: Sprinkle salad seeds thinly on a pot of compost, cover lightly and water.
Keep it somewhere bright. Water it when the soil feels dry.
When the leaves are as long as your finger, snip some for tea.

quests.title: Make real lemonade and get the sweetness just right
quests.why: Real lemonade is sour, sweet and cold. You choose the balance.
steps: A grown-up cuts the lemons in half. You squeeze out every drop.
Stir in a little sugar, then cold water, and taste.
Too sour? Add sugar. Too sweet? Add lemon. Serve it with ice.

quests.title: Make Eton mess: crush, chop, fold and serve
quests.why: A pudding that’s meant to look messy.
steps: Crush meringues in a bag into big crumbs.
Chop strawberries with a table knife.
Fold it all into yoghurt or whipped cream and spoon it into glasses.

quests.title: Blindfold taste test: guess five summer fruits
quests.why: Your nose does half the tasting. Find out how good yours is.
steps: Ask a grown-up to cut five fruits into small pieces.
Blindfold on, taste each one and guess.
Swap: you do the feeding and they guess. Who got more?

quests.title: Summer bake-off: same biscuit dough, your own design
quests.why: Same dough, different ideas. That’s where it gets interesting.
steps: Make one batch of biscuit dough together, with a grown-up for the oven.
Split it. You each shape and decorate your own.
A grown-up tastes them without knowing whose is whose, and picks a winner.

quests.title: Cook lunch for everyone from three things in season in August
quests.why: August is when British fruit and vegetables are at their best.
steps: Find three things in season now: courgettes, tomatoes, sweetcorn, beans or plums.
Plan a lunch around them and cook it. A grown-up does the hob and oven, and stays beside you for anything sharp.
Serve it, and tell everyone what’s in season.

quests.title: Make a day-out bingo card and fill it on the way
quests.why: Long trips go faster when you’re hunting for something.
steps: Draw nine squares. In each one, put something you might see: a cow, a red car, a bridge.
Take it on the journey and tick each one you spot.
A full card wins. Make a harder one for the way home.

quests.title: Follow a waymarked trail all the way round
quests.why: Little arrows on posts lead somewhere. Follow them to the end.
steps: Pick a trail at a forest, a country park or a nature reserve, with a grown-up.
Be the one who spots each waymark post and the next arrow.
Finish the whole loop. Say which bit was best.

quests.title: Museum detective: find the oldest thing in the building
quests.why: Museums are full of things older than anyone you know.
steps: Visit a museum with a grown-up. Lots of them are free.
Hunt for the oldest thing, reading the labels as you go.
Draw it and write how old it is.

quests.title: Make a lost plan before a busy day out
quests.why: Knowing what to do if you get lost makes a busy place feel smaller.
steps: When you arrive, agree a meeting spot with your grown-up.
If you lose each other, stand still and look for someone who works there.
Know your grown-up’s phone number, or carry it written down.

quests.title: Pack a boredom-buster bag for a long journey
quests.why: A good journey bag means fewer “are we nearly there yet?”
steps: Think about who is coming and what they like.
Pack a game, a snack and something quiet for each person.
Hand them round when the journey starts.

quests.title: Rainy day out: waterproofs on, and find the biggest puddle
quests.why: Rain doesn’t cancel a day out. It just makes it wetter.
steps: Waterproofs and wellies on, a grown-up along.
Walk until you find the biggest puddle.
Measure it in jumps, then home to get dry.

quests.title: Send a postcard from somewhere you went this summer
quests.why: A postcard is a little bit of your day, posted to someone else.
steps: Choose or make a postcard of somewhere you went, with a grown-up.
Write three things you did, and draw something small.
Post it to someone who would love some post.

quests.title: Paint kindness pebbles and leave them on a walk for people to find
quests.why: Finding a kind word on a pebble can make someone’s whole day.
steps: Paint smooth pebbles in bright colours, with one kind word on each.
Let them dry. A grown-up can seal them with clear varnish.
Leave them along a walk, where a grown-up says it’s OK.

quests.title: Hot day helper: keep everyone at home cool
quests.why: Heat is hard on babies, older people and pets. You can help.
steps: Fill a water bottle for everyone at home and put them in the fridge.
Close the curtains in rooms the sun shines into.
Check any pets have shade and fresh water.

quests.title: Make a summer box for someone who can’t get out much
quests.why: Summer can be lonely if you’re stuck indoors.
steps: With a grown-up, think of someone who doesn’t get out much.
Fill a box with summer: a drawing, a flower, a puzzle, a letter.
Drop it round together.

quests.title: Kindness tag: do a kind thing, then pass it on
quests.why: Kindness spreads faster when it’s a game.
steps: One of you starts by doing something kind for the other.
Now it’s their turn to do one back and pass it on.
Keep it going all day. A grown-up counts the kind things.

quests.title: Be kind to your body: a slow hour in the shade on a hot day
quests.why: Hot days wear you out. Resting is the clever part.
steps: Find shade: under a tree, a parasol, or indoors with the curtains shut.
Lie down with water and a book or some music.
An hour of slow. Save running about for when it’s cooler.

quests.title: Water a neighbour’s plants while they’re on holiday
quests.why: Plants can’t go on holiday. Someone has to stay and help.
steps: With a grown-up, offer to look after a neighbour’s plants while they’re away.
Go round together and water them on the days you agreed.
Leave a note for when they get back, saying how the plants got on.

quests.title: Run a mini sports day for younger children in the family
quests.why: Little ones love a sports day. Running one is a big job.
steps: Plan four easy races: egg and spoon, sack, hopping and a welly throw.
Set it up with a grown-up there, and explain each race simply.
Cheer everyone on, and give every runner a medal you made.

quests.title: Make a summer time capsule to open next summer
quests.why: By next summer you’ll have forgotten half of this. Now you won’t.
steps: Find a tin or a box with a lid.
Put in a drawing, a ticket, a list of your favourite things and a note to open next year.
Seal it, write the date to open it on the lid, and hide it somewhere safe.

quests.title: Host the family summer awards, with an award for everyone
quests.why: Everyone did something good this summer. Say what.
steps: Think up an award for each person at home: best splash, best laugh, best picnic.
Make the awards from card, foil and ribbon.
Hold the ceremony and read out why each one won.

quests.title: Go further than ever: your longest walk or ride of the summer
quests.why: The end of summer is a good time to find out how far your legs can go.
steps: Pick a route with a grown-up that’s longer than anything you’ve done.
Pack water and a snack, and set off together.
Finish it, then work out how far you went.

quests.title: Plan the grand finale party together: food, music and one game
quests.why: A big summer deserves a big ending.
steps: Together, choose the food, the music and one game everyone can play.
Share out the jobs, and make invitations for everyone at home.
Throw the party, and play the game until someone wins.

quests.title: Put summer away: wash, dry and pack the summer kit
quests.why: Next summer starts better when the buckets aren’t mouldy.
steps: Gather the summer things: buckets, the paddling pool, water bottles, sun hats.
Wash and dry each one properly.
Pack them away together, where you’ll find them next year.

quests.title: Move bedtime earlier for school: fifteen minutes earlier, three nights
quests.why: Your body clock moves slowly. Give it a few nights’ warning.
steps: With a grown-up, agree a bedtime fifteen minutes earlier than now.
Screens off half an hour before, then lights out on time.
Three nights in a row. Move it again if you need to.

quests.title: Bake a finale cake and decorate it with your best summer moment
quests.why: Every grand finale needs a cake.
steps: Bake a simple sponge with a grown-up, who does the oven.
Let it cool, then plan the top: your best moment of the summer.
Decorate it, then share it out.

quests.title: Light up the longest night with fairy lights or a torch
quests.why: 21 December has more dark than any other day. Fill it with light.
steps: On or near 21 December, turn the big lights off after tea.
Light the room with fairy lights, torches or battery candles.
Tell or read a story by the glow.

quests.title: Make three decorations from things you already have
quests.why: The best decorations are the ones somebody made.
steps: Gather card, old wrapping paper, pine cones, string or ribbon.
Make three: a paper chain, a star and a hanging pine cone.
Hang them up where everyone will see.

quests.title: Wrap a present so neatly nobody can guess what it is
quests.why: Good wrapping is half the surprise.
steps: Cut the paper so it just goes round, with a little spare.
Fold the ends into triangles and tape them flat.
Add a tag in your best writing.

quests.title: Bake gingerbread and decorate one for each person at home
quests.why: A gingerbread person can look like anyone you know.
steps: Make the dough with a grown-up, who does the oven.
Roll it out and cut one shape for each person at home.
Decorate each one to look like its person.

quests.title: Make a secret present together for a grown-up at home
quests.why: Two people keeping one secret is harder than it sounds.
steps: Together, pick a grown-up and decide what to make: a card, a picture, a jar of treats.
Make it while they’re busy. One of you keeps watch.
Give it together, and see if they guessed.

quests.title: Make an ice suncatcher and hang it in a tree
quests.why: On a frosty night, water turns into a window.
steps: Put leaves, twigs, orange slices and a loop of string in a shallow tray of water.
Leave it outside on a frosty night, or in the freezer.
Pop it out and hang it up outside. How long does it last?

quests.title: Find Orion’s belt on a clear winter evening
quests.why: Winter nights come early, so the stars are out before bedtime.
steps: On a clear evening, wrap up and go outside with a grown-up.
Look for three bright stars in a short, straight line. That’s Orion’s belt.
Find the hunter around it: two shoulders and two feet.

quests.title: Paper snowball fight: fewest snowballs on your side wins
quests.why: No snow? No problem.
steps: Scrunch up old paper into twenty snowballs each.
A line down the middle of the room. A grown-up starts the music.
Throw them over the line. When the music stops, fewest on your side wins.

quests.title: Keep the birds’ water from freezing on five cold mornings
quests.why: Birds need to drink and bathe in winter too, and their water freezes.
steps: Put out a shallow dish of water where you can see it from a window.
Each cold morning, check it. If it’s frozen, a grown-up pours in some warm water, never salt.
Watch who comes to drink.

quests.title: Roll a pine cone in seeds and hang it for the birds
quests.why: Winter is the hungriest time for garden birds.
steps: A grown-up spreads lard on a pine cone and ties string to the top.
Roll it in bird seed until it’s covered.
Hang it outside where you can watch from a window.

quests.title: Write three hopes for the new year and seal them in an envelope
quests.why: Hopes are easier to chase once they’re written down.
steps: Think of three hopes: one for you, one for home, one for the world.
Write or draw them, and seal them in an envelope.
Write “Open next December” on the front and keep it somewhere safe.

quests.title: Make a family top ten of the year together
quests.why: A whole year is a lot. Here’s where you find the best of it.
steps: Together, look back over the year, month by month.
Each pick five best moments. Tiny ones count.
Put all ten in order and read out the number one.

quests.title: Learn to say happy new year in five languages
quests.why: Lots of people celebrate the new year, in lots of different words.
steps: With a grown-up, find out how to say happy new year in five languages.
Practise until you can say them all without looking.
Say all five to someone at breakfast.

quests.title: Take the decorations down and pack them carefully for next year
quests.why: Next year, someone will thank you for no tangled lights.
steps: Take down the decorations you can reach from the floor. A grown-up does anything high.
Wrap the breakable ones in paper and wind the lights round a piece of card.
Label the box so it’s easy to find next year.

quests.title: First walk of the year: somewhere you’ve never been
quests.why: Start the year by going somewhere new.
steps: Near New Year’s Day, pick somewhere new to walk with a grown-up.
Walk it together, wrapped up warm.
Find one thing to remember it by: a view, a leaf, a funny sign.

quests.title: Egg and spoon race: first over the line with the egg still on
quests.why: Fast is easy. Fast and steady is the trick.
steps: A hard-boiled or a plastic egg and a spoon each.
Mark a start and a finish, outside or down the hall.
Drop it and you go back to the start. Best of three.

quests.title: Egg drop: build a case that keeps a raw egg safe from a fall
quests.why: Engineers design things that survive a fall. So can you.
steps: Build a case for a raw egg from straws, card, paper and tape.
Outside, a grown-up drops it from the top step onto newspaper.
Did it crack? Change one thing and test again.

quests.title: Visit a farm in spring and count the baby animals
quests.why: Spring is when farms fill up with lambs, chicks and calves.
steps: Visit an open farm with a grown-up.
Find and count every kind of baby animal.
Wash your hands with soap and water after, and say which was your favourite.

quests.title: Make chocolate nests and put three little eggs in each
quests.why: Crunchy, chocolatey and about the easiest thing you’ll ever make.
steps: A grown-up melts the chocolate. You stir in the cornflakes.
Spoon it into cake cases and press a dip in the middle.
Add three little eggs to each nest and let them set.

quests.title: Eat one small chocolate egg as slowly as you possibly can
quests.why: Slow chocolate tastes twice as good. Find out.
steps: Sit down with one small chocolate egg, or another small treat.
Look at it, smell it, then let a piece melt on your tongue.
Make it last two whole minutes. Say what you noticed.

quests.title: Leave out nest-building things for the birds
quests.why: Birds are building nests now, hunting for soft things.
steps: Collect natural bits: moss, dry grass, small twigs and feathers.
Pack them into an old fat-ball feeder or a mesh bag. Never string or wool.
Hang it near a bush and watch who comes to collect.

quests.title: Visit a pond, look for tadpoles and draw what you see
quests.why: In spring, ponds fill up with tiny wriggling tadpoles.
steps: Go to a pond with a grown-up, who stays right beside you.
Kneel on the bank and look in the shallow edges. Look, don’t scoop.
Draw the tadpoles. Go back in a few weeks to look for legs.

quests.title: Plant potatoes in a bag and dig them up in the summer
quests.why: Plant one potato now and dig up a whole handful in July.
steps: Fill a big bag or tub a third full with compost and plant two seed potatoes.
When shoots show, cover them with more compost, until the bag is full.
Water it when it’s dry. Dig in when the flowers open, in summer.

quests.title: Find a tree in blossom and have a snack underneath it
quests.why: In Japan, families picnic under blossom trees. It only lasts a few weeks.
steps: Go blossom hunting with a grown-up.
Find the best tree in blossom and sit under it with a snack.
Lie back for five minutes and watch the petals.

quests.title: Make a wormery in a jar and watch the worms dig
quests.why: Worms are the garden’s quiet workers. Watch them at it.
steps: Layer soil and sand in a big jar, with leaves on top. Add a few worms.
Wrap it in dark paper and keep it somewhere cool. Peek on three days.
After a week, put the worms back where you found them.

quests.title: Make a rain gauge and measure the April showers
quests.why: April is famous for showers. Find out how much really falls.
steps: A grown-up cuts the top off a plastic bottle. Turn it upside down in the bottle as a funnel.
Mark a scale on the side with a ruler, and stand it outside away from trees.
Check it at the same time each day and write down the rain.

quests.title: Give your bike its spring check: tyres, brakes and chain
quests.why: A bike that’s been parked all winter needs a once-over.
steps: Pump up the tyres with a grown-up until they feel firm.
Squeeze both brakes. Do they stop the wheels?
Wipe the chain and add a drop of oil. Then a test ride with a grown-up.

quests.title: Play out in the first light evening after the clocks go forward
quests.why: The clocks have gone forward. The evenings are yours again.
steps: After tea, notice it’s still light outside.
Get out with a grown-up for a game, a ride or a run.
Come in when it starts to get dark, and say what you played.

quests.title: Fold a paper boat and sail it in a puddle
quests.why: Rain makes little seas everywhere, if you look.
steps: Fold a boat from a sheet of paper. Colour it in first.
Wellies on, find a big puddle with a grown-up.
Sail it and blow it across. How far does it get before it sinks?

quests.title: Wake early and listen to the birds singing at sunrise
quests.why: In spring, birds sing loudest just as the sun comes up.
steps: Wake as early as you can, then open the window or step outside with a grown-up.
Sit still and listen for five minutes.
Count how many different songs you can hear.

quests.title: Learn to fix a bike puncture
quests.why: A flat tyre is a twenty-minute fix once you know how.
steps: With a grown-up, take the wheel off and lever the tyre and inner tube out.
Pump the tube up, find the hole by listening or in a bowl of water, and patch it.
Put it all back, pump it up and check it holds.

quests.title: Give your toys a spring bath
quests.why: Toys get grubby over the winter. Give them a wash.
steps: Fill a bowl with warm soapy water.
Wash your plastic toys with a sponge and rinse them.
Line them up on a towel to dry.

quests.title: Plant bulbs now for flowers in the spring
quests.why: Bulbs planted in autumn sleep all winter and come up in spring.
steps: Get some daffodil or crocus bulbs with a grown-up.
Plant each one three times as deep as it is tall, pointy end up.
Water them, mark the spot, and wash your hands after.

quests.title: Fungi hunt: find five toadstools or mushrooms, look but never touch
quests.why: Autumn is when mushrooms pop up overnight.
steps: Go to the woods or the park with a grown-up.
Look at the bottoms of trees, on old logs and in the grass.
Find five and draw them. Look, but never touch or pick them.

quests.title: Hunt for conkers and play a proper game of conkers
quests.why: A shiny conker straight out of its shell is one of autumn’s best finds.
steps: Hunt under horse chestnut trees with a grown-up. Conkers are for playing, never eating.
A grown-up makes a hole in your best one and threads it on a string.
Take turns to swing at each other’s conker. Hold yours out at arm’s length.

quests.title: The clocks go back: spend the extra hour on something slow
quests.why: Once a year you get a whole extra hour. Choose what it’s for.
steps: The clocks go back an hour on the last Sunday in October.
Plan the extra hour: a long breakfast, a book, a game, a lie-in.
Spend it slowly, then help change any clocks that don’t change themselves.

quests.title: Find out why leaves change colour, and explain it at tea
quests.why: Green leaves hide their yellow and orange all summer.
steps: With a grown-up, find out what chlorophyll is and why it fades in autumn.
Collect a green, a yellow and a red leaf to show it.
Explain it at tea in under a minute.

quests.title: Make a pine cone weather station
quests.why: Pine cones close up when it’s damp and open when it’s dry.
steps: Collect a few pine cones on an autumn walk.
Put one outside and one inside.
Look at them each day for three days. Which one opened?

quests.title: Race sycamore helicopters and find the slowest spinner
quests.why: Sycamore seeds spin like tiny helicopters so they land far from their tree.
steps: Collect a handful of sycamore seeds, the ones with wings.
Drop them from the same height, one at a time.
Find the one that takes longest to land.

quests.title: Be a squirrel: hide ten conkers or acorns, and find them tomorrow
quests.why: Squirrels hide nuts in autumn and have to remember where.
steps: Collect ten conkers or acorns. They’re for hiding, never eating.
Hide them around the garden or a room, one at a time.
Tomorrow, find them all. How many did you remember?

quests.title: Build a nest box with a grown-up, ready for nesting season
quests.why: Birds start house-hunting in February. Have a home ready.
steps: Build a nest box from a kit or a plan with a grown-up, who does any sawing.
Choose a spot one to three metres up, facing between north and east, out of the hot sun.
A grown-up fixes it up. Watch from a window for visitors.

quests.title: Keep a half-term weather diary: draw the sky each day
quests.why: February weather changes every day. Catch all of it.
steps: Draw a box for each day of half-term.
Each day, look out at the same time and draw the sky.
Add how cold it felt and which coat you needed.

quests.title: Play Poohsticks on a bridge over a stream
quests.why: Drop, dash to the other side, and see whose stick wins.
steps: Find a footbridge over a stream with a grown-up. No leaning over the rail.
Each pick a stick and drop it on the side the water comes from, at the same time.
Dash across and see whose comes out first. Best of five.

quests.title: Make a rice sock warmer for cold hands
quests.why: Cold hands make everything harder. Warm ones help you settle.
steps: Fill an old clean sock with dry rice and tie a tight knot.
A grown-up warms it in the microwave and checks it’s warm, not hot.
Hold it, breathe slowly and let your hands thaw.

quests.title: Chit seed potatoes in an egg box, ready for spring
quests.why: Potatoes woken up in February are ready to plant at Easter.
steps: Get some seed potatoes with a grown-up.
Stand each one in an egg box, the end with the most little eyes pointing up.
Keep them somewhere cool and light. Look each week for short green shoots.

quests.title: Put on a shadow puppet show with a torch
quests.why: Dark afternoons are perfect for shadows.
steps: Cut animal shapes from card and tape them to sticks.
Shine a torch at a wall or a sheet in a dark room.
Act out a story, with voices, for someone at home.

quests.title: Windy day dash: run into the wind, then with it
quests.why: Running into the wind is hard. Running with it feels like flying.
steps: On a windy day, find an open space with a grown-up.
Run into the wind to a marker, then turn and run back with it.
Time both ways. How much did the wind help?

quests.title: Half-term games league: three games, a table and a champion
quests.why: One game is luck. Three games is a league.
steps: Pick three games together: a card game, a board game and one you make up.
Play them all. Three points for a win, one for a draw, on a table you draw.
Crown the champion. Shake hands, whoever wins.

quests.title: Cook a winter warmer for the family, a grown-up beside you
quests.why: A pot of something hot on a cold February night goes down well.
steps: Pick a stew, a soup or a curry and check the ingredients with a grown-up.
Chop and cook it, with a grown-up beside you at the hob.
Serve it, and ask everyone for one thing to change next time.

quests.title: Go on a problem hunt: five small annoying things at home
quests.why: Every invention starts with something that bugs someone.
steps: Walk round your home with a notebook and look for small everyday annoyances: a lid that rolls away, a cable that tangles, shoes in a heap.
Write or draw five of them, and who each one bothers.
Circle the one you most want to solve. That’s your problem to invent for.

quests.title: Interview two people at home about your problem
quests.why: Inventors ask the people who’ll use it before they build anything.
steps: Pick two people at home who the problem bothers.
Ask them three questions: when does it happen, what have you tried, and what would make it better?
Write down their answers, and one thing that surprised you.

quests.title: Design detective: find out how an everyday thing got better
quests.why: One inventor built 5,127 prototypes of a vacuum cleaner before one worked. Most good things took many goes.
steps: Pick something at home that has changed over the years: a phone, a toothbrush, a torch, a bike.
Ask a grown-up what theirs was like at your age, and what annoyed them about it.
List three changes the designers made, and the problem each one solved.

quests.title: Set up your workshop box from clean recycling
quests.why: Real workshops keep everything where you can find it.
steps: Ask a grown-up which clean boxes, tubes, bottle tops and lids you can keep.
Add the tools you’re allowed: scissors, tape, string, pegs, elastic bands, and split pins if you have them.
Sort it all into one big box and label the outside.

quests.title: Learn five ways to join cardboard without glue
quests.why: Know your joins and your invention holds together.
steps: On scrap card, try a slot, a tab pushed through a slit, a tape hinge, a split pin and a string tie. A grown-up pokes any holes.
Test each one: does it bend, turn or hold still?
Keep your five samples and label what each one is good for.

quests.title: Build a cardboard grabber that can pick up a sock
quests.why: A warm-up build. Every inventor starts by making something that moves.
steps: Cut two long strips of card the same size and join them at one end with tape or a split pin. A grown-up cuts any thick card.
Give the far ends a grip: folded card, pegs or bottle tops.
Test it on a sock, a pencil and a teddy, then make the grip better.

quests.title: Sketch ten ideas in ten minutes, then pick one
quests.why: The first idea is rarely the best one. The seventh might be.
steps: Fold a page into ten boxes and set a timer for ten minutes.
Sketch one quick idea for your problem in each box. Silly ones count.
Star your favourite and your wildest, and talk them through with a grown-up.

quests.title: Draw your design with labels and real measurements
quests.why: A good drawing shows anyone how it works before it exists.
steps: Draw your chosen idea big, from the front and from the side.
Label every part and what it’s made from.
Measure the space it has to fit, and write the sizes on your drawing.

quests.title: Find out which material keeps a toy dry in the rain
quests.why: Inventors test their materials before they use them.
steps: Find four things to try as a roof: paper, foil, a plastic bag and a bit of cloth.
Wrap a tissue in each, then sprinkle water on with your fingers, over the sink.
Unwrap them. Which kept the tissue driest? Give the winner a tick.

quests.title: Run a fair test to choose the best material
quests.why: A fair test changes one thing at a time, so you know what made the difference.
steps: Pick what your invention needs most: strength, grip, waterproofing or bendiness.
Test three materials the same way and the same size, changing only the material.
Record the results in a table and choose your winner.

quests.title: Build your prototype: a quick model first, then the real one
quests.why: A rough model shows up the problems while they’re still easy to fix.
steps: Day one: make a rough model in twenty minutes from paper and tape, just to check the idea.
Day two: build the real one from your recycling, using your best joins. A grown-up cuts any thick card or plastic.
Check it against your drawing and note anything you changed.

quests.title: Test your invention three times and log what goes wrong
quests.why: When something goes wrong in a test, the test is working.
steps: Use your invention for real, the way it’s meant to be used, three times.
After each go, write what worked, what wobbled and what broke.
Ask someone else to try it once, and watch without helping.

quests.title: Make version two: fix the biggest problem and test again
quests.why: Version two is where inventions get good.
steps: Look at your test log, or try your invention once more, and pick the biggest problem.
Change one thing to fix it: a stronger join, a better grip, a new shape.
Test it again, and write v2 on it if it works better.

quests.title: Write your invention’s patent page
quests.why: A patent explains what is new about an idea so clearly that someone else could make it.
steps: Give your invention a name, and write one sentence on the problem it solves.
Draw it with numbered parts, and explain how each part works.
Finish with what makes it new: the one thing nothing else at home does.

quests.title: Demo day: show the family what you invented
quests.why: Inventors show their work. Today the family sees what you made, and why.
steps: Set up a demo table with your invention, your drawing and your test log, and invite everyone.
Explain the problem, show how it works, and tell them what you changed in version two.
Let each person have a go, then take their questions.

quests.title: Make your detective casebook and kit
quests.why: Good detectives write down what they find, the moment they find it.
steps: Fold and staple some paper into a notebook, or use an old one, and give it a case number on the cover.
Pack a kit: a pencil, a ruler, a magnifying glass if you have one, and a clear tub that a grown-up pokes air holes in.
Rule up your first page: date, place, what I saw, what I think.

quests.title: Case one: who nibbled this leaf?
quests.why: Leaf-eaters leave bite marks, a bit like fingerprints.
steps: With a grown-up, find five nibbled leaves in a garden, a park, a street tree or a pot plant.
Read the bites: holes in the middle often mean slugs or snails, scoops from the edge often mean caterpillars, and wiggly pale lines mean a tiny grub living inside.
Draw each leaf in your casebook and write your best guess for the nibbler.

quests.title: Make a wanted poster for the leaf nibbler
quests.why: Detectives tell everyone what to look out for.
steps: Pick the nibbler you think is out there: a snail, a slug or a caterpillar.
Draw it big, with the words: Wanted, for nibbling leaves.
Add a clue: where it was last seen and what it likes to eat.

quests.title: Find five signs that an animal has been here
quests.why: Animals hide from us, but they leave clues behind.
steps: With a grown-up, search a garden, a park or a path for signs: a feather, a footprint in mud, a chewed nut or cone, a hole, a trail.
Look closely, but don’t touch droppings or anything dead, and leave everything where it is.
Draw each clue and write which animal you think left it.

quests.title: Case two: where do the snails go in the day?
quests.why: Snails come out when it’s damp and dark. In the day they vanish. Where to?
steps: Day one, in daylight, with a grown-up: search under pots, along walls, in ivy and damp corners, and note every snail hiding place.
Day two, on a damp evening: go back with a grown-up and a torch and look again.
Compare the two and write where they hide and where they go. Wash your hands after.

quests.title: Set out an ant picnic and find out what ants like best
quests.why: Ants send out scouts to find food. Watch which crumb wins.
steps: With a grown-up, find some ants outside, on a path or by a wall.
Put three tiny crumbs on a bit of card near them: a grain of sugar, a crumb of bread and a scrap of apple.
Watch for ten minutes. Which one do they find first, and which do they carry away?

quests.title: Case three: where does a puddle go?
quests.why: Puddles disappear without anyone drinking them. Time to find out how.
steps: After rain, find a puddle on a path, a patio or a balcony, with a grown-up. No puddle? Pour a little water on a tray instead.
Draw round its edge with chalk, or with a pen on the tray, and again every hour.
Watch the rings shrink. Write your guess for where the water went, then check it with a grown-up.

quests.title: Case four: whose web is this? Find three different kinds
quests.why: Each kind of spider builds its own shape of web. The web tells you who made it.
steps: On a misty or dewy morning, look along fences, hedges, sheds and window frames with a grown-up.
Find three shapes: a wheel, a flat sheet and a messy tangle.
Sketch each one and where it was. Look, and leave the web whole.

quests.title: Take a ten-minute safari in one crack in a pavement or a wall
quests.why: A crack in a wall can be a whole jungle, if you look small enough.
steps: With a grown-up, pick one crack in a pavement, a wall or some steps, away from traffic.
Look closely for ten minutes: moss, tiny plants, ants, spiders, woodlice.
Count everything that lives there and draw a map of the crack.

quests.title: Case five: which birds visit? A ten-minute stakeout on three days
quests.why: Birds keep a timetable. Watch at the same time each day and you’ll learn it.
steps: Pick a window with a view of a tree, a roof, a garden or a feeder, and the same time each day.
Sit still for ten minutes and tally every bird. Don’t know its name? Note its colour, size and what it did.
After three days, work out who visits most, and when.

quests.title: Build a choice chamber: do woodlice like it damp or dry?
quests.why: Scientists ask animals questions by giving them a choice.
steps: With a grown-up, find ten woodlice under logs, pots or stones, and move them gently into a tub with a little leaf litter.
In a tray, put damp kitchen roll at one end and dry at the other. Put the woodlice in the middle, cover it and wait ten minutes.
Count where they went and try once more, then put every woodlouse back where you found it and wash your hands.

quests.title: Moth night: light up a white sheet and see who comes
quests.why: The UK has about 2,500 kinds of moth, and most of them fly at night, unseen.
steps: After dark, with a grown-up, hang a white sheet over a washing line, a chair or a balcony rail and shine a bright torch or a battery lantern on it.
Check it every ten minutes for an hour. Look closely, but never touch the wings.
Count and draw every moth and other visitor, then switch off the light so they can go.

quests.title: Adopt a tree and visit it once a week for three weeks
quests.why: A tree changes every week, but you only see it if you keep coming back.
steps: With a grown-up, choose a tree near home: in a garden, a park or on your street.
Each visit, do one thing: a bark rubbing, a leaf drawing, a count of who lives on it, a note of what has changed.
After three visits, give your tree its own casebook page with everything you found.

quests.title: Make a yes or no key that tells six of your finds apart
quests.why: Naturalists use keys: a chain of yes or no questions that ends at a name.
steps: Pick six things you’ve found or drawn: leaves, birds, minibeasts or webs.
Write one yes or no question that splits them into two groups, like: does it have more than six legs? Keep splitting until each one stands alone.
Test your key on someone at home: they pick one in secret, and your questions find it.

quests.title: Make your own field guide to the wildlife near your home
quests.why: Nobody else has a guide to your patch. Now there is one, and you wrote it.
steps: Pick at least eight living things from your cases: birds, minibeasts, trees, plants, webs.
Give each one a page: a drawing, where to find it, when, and one clue for spotting it.
Make a cover and a map of your patch, then give the family a tour of your guide.

quests.title: Catch story seeds: ten what-if questions
quests.why: Every story starts with a what-if.
steps: Fold a page into ten boxes.
In each one, write a what-if: what if the cat could talk, what if the stairs went somewhere new, what if it never got dark.
Star the one you can’t stop thinking about. That’s your story seed.

quests.title: Invent your main character: what they want and what scares them
quests.why: A character who wants something is a character people follow.
steps: Draw your main character and give them a name.
Write what they want more than anything, and what they’re scared of.
Add one thing that makes them them: a saying, a hat, something they always carry.

quests.title: Make the trouble: a villain, a rival or a big problem
quests.why: Without trouble there’s no story, just a nice day.
steps: Decide what stands in your hero’s way: a villain, a rival, a storm or something lost.
Draw it and give it a name.
Write why it wants to stop your hero, or how it gets in the way.

quests.title: Write one scene from your villain’s side
quests.why: The best villains think they’re the hero of their own story.
steps: Pick a moment where your hero and your villain or rival clash. No villain yet? Invent one first.
Write the scene from the villain’s side: what they want, and why they think they’re right.
Note one thing you learned that changes how you’ll write them.

quests.title: Build your story’s world: a map and three rules
quests.why: Readers believe in a world that has its own rules.
steps: Draw a map of where your story happens, a town, a planet, a house or a forest, and mark three places your hero will go.
Write three rules of this world, like: nobody can lie here, or the river only flows at night.
Mark the spot where your story starts.

quests.title: Plot it on a story mountain in five boxes
quests.why: A story climbs up to its big moment, then comes back down.
steps: Draw a mountain with five boxes: the start, the problem, the build-up, the big moment and the ending.
Write or draw one line in each box.
Tell the whole story to someone in one minute, using only your mountain.

quests.title: Choose your format: a comic, a zine, a little book or an audio story
quests.why: The same story feels different as a comic, a zine or a story you listen to.
steps: Pick how your story will be made: a comic, a zine, a little book or an audio story.
Make a dummy, a blank practice copy: fold or staple the pages, or for audio, write a running order.
Pencil in what goes on each page or in each part, so you know it all fits.

quests.title: Act your story out with toys to see if it works
quests.why: Moving the characters round shows you the bits that are missing.
steps: Pick a toy for each character, and a box or a rug for your world.
Act out the whole story, doing all the voices.
Find one bit that felt too quick, and add something to it.

quests.title: Make five sound effects for your story from kitchen things
quests.why: On the radio, horses’ hooves were often two coconut halves. Sounds can be made from anything.
steps: Pick five sounds your story needs: footsteps, rain, a door, wind, a monster.
Find ways to make them: rice shaken in a tub for rain, a scrunched crisp packet for fire, flapping gloves for wings.
Play them while someone reads a page, and keep the ones that sound best.

quests.title: Make your story over three days, one part a day
quests.why: Big stories get made a bit at a time.
steps: Day one: make the beginning, up to where the trouble starts. For an audio story, record on a grown-up’s phone, with their OK.
Day two: make the middle, where things get harder for your hero.
Day three: make the big moment. Leave the very end for later.

quests.title: Write two different endings, then choose one
quests.why: The ending is what readers remember, so it’s worth trying more than one.
steps: Write or draw an ending where your hero gets what they wanted.
Write or draw another where they get something different, maybe something better.
Read both to someone, then choose one and finish your story.

quests.title: Read your story aloud and fix three things
quests.why: Your ears catch what your eyes skip.
steps: Read your whole story out loud, slowly, with a pencil in your hand.
Mark anywhere you stumble, get bored or feel confused.
Fix the three biggest: cut a slow bit, add a missing clue or sharpen something a character says.

quests.title: Show, don’t tell: rewrite one flat sentence three ways
quests.why: ‘Sam was scared’ tells you. ‘Sam’s hands wouldn’t stop shaking’ shows you.
steps: Find a sentence in your story that tells a feeling: they were angry, it was scary, the room felt sad.
Rewrite it three ways that show it instead: what someone does, what they say, what we notice.
Keep the best one in your story.

quests.title: Design the cover, the title and the blurb on the back
quests.why: People pick up a story because of its cover.
steps: Choose a title that makes people curious.
Design the front: the title, a picture and your name as the author. A made-up pen name is fine too.
On the back, write three lines that make people want to read it, without giving away the ending.

quests.title: Launch day: a reading of your story for the family
quests.why: Authors launch their books with a reading. Today it’s yours.
steps: Make invitations and set up a reading spot: chairs, your story, and a glass of water for the author.
Read your story aloud, or play your audio story, doing the voices and the sound effects.
Take questions from the audience, then sign a copy or a bookmark for someone.

quests.title: Find the brightest growing spot in your home
quests.why: Plants feed on light. The brightest spot grows the strongest plants.
steps: Pick three possible spots: a windowsill, a balcony, a doorstep or a corner of a garden.
Check each one in the morning, at lunchtime and after school: is it in sun, bright shade or dark?
Choose the one with the most light, and ask a grown-up if it can be your growing spot.

quests.title: Make plant pots from things heading for the recycling
quests.why: A yoghurt pot or an egg box can be a seed’s first home.
steps: Collect clean pots, tubs, egg boxes and cardboard tubes.
A grown-up makes a few small holes in the bottom of each, so water can drain.
Stand them on a tray or an old lid, and make a label for each.

quests.title: Build a self-watering pot from a plastic bottle
quests.why: A wick pulls water up to the roots, so your plant can drink while you’re at school.
steps: A grown-up cuts a big plastic bottle in half and makes a hole in the cap.
Thread a strip of old cloth or a shoelace through the cap so it hangs down into the bottom half.
Turn the top half upside down into the bottom, fill it with soil and pour water into the base.

quests.title: Go on a seed hunt in the kitchen cupboards
quests.why: Lots of the food in your kitchen is seeds, and some of them will still grow.
steps: With a grown-up, look for seeds: whole dried peas, lentils and chickpeas (split ones won’t grow), mustard seeds in the spice rack, pips in fruit, seeds inside a pepper or a tomato.
Line them up from smallest to biggest and look closely at each one.
Pick two to try growing, and ask a grown-up if you can use some.

quests.title: Sow your crop: cress, pea shoots, herbs or a sunflower
quests.why: This is the one you’ll look after, measure and share at the end.
steps: Choose your crop: cress or mustard seeds, dried peas soaked overnight for pea shoots, herb seeds, or in spring a sunflower seed.
Sow them on damp kitchen roll or soil, press them in gently and sprinkle them with water.
Label the pot with the name and the date, and put it in your growing spot.

quests.title: Keep a grow diary: one page a week for three weeks
quests.why: Plants grow too slowly to watch. A diary catches it.
steps: Start your diary with the date, what you sowed and where.
Once a week, draw your plant life size and write one thing that changed.
After three weeks, flick back through. Can you see it grow?

quests.title: Grow a bean in a jar and watch its roots
quests.why: Roots grow in the dark, under the soil. In a jar, you get to see them.
steps: Line a clear jar or plastic cup with damp kitchen roll, and slide a dried bean, pea or chickpea between the paper and the side.
Keep the paper damp and the jar somewhere light. This one is for watching, not eating.
Draw it on three days: when the root comes out, when the shoot appears, and which way each one grows.

quests.title: Plant pips from the fruit bowl and see if they wake up
quests.why: Every pip is a tiny plant, waiting.
steps: Save some pips or seeds from a tomato, a pepper, a lemon or an orange.
Push them just under the soil in a pot, water them and stand a clear tub over the top to keep them warm and damp.
Check every few days. Which ones wake up first?

quests.title: Regrow a carrot top or a lettuce stump in a saucer of water
quests.why: Some vegetables grow back from the bit we usually throw away.
steps: Ask a grown-up to cut you the top of a carrot, the base of a lettuce or the bottom of a celery bunch.
Stand it cut side down in a saucer with a little water, in your growing spot.
Change the water every two days. After a week, how much has grown back?

quests.title: Light or dark: run a fair test on two pots
quests.why: Gardeners say plants need light. Test it for yourself.
steps: Sow two pots exactly the same: the same seeds, the same soil or kitchen roll, the same water.
Put one in your growing spot and one in a dark cupboard, and water both the same.
After a week, compare their height, colour and leaves. What did the light do?

quests.title: Measure your seedlings on five days and make a growth chart
quests.why: Numbers show you what your eyes miss.
steps: Pick your tallest seedling and stand a ruler or a paper strip beside it.
On five days, measure it in millimetres and write down the day.
Draw a bar chart with one bar a day. Which day did it grow most?

quests.title: Thin out your seedlings so the strongest have room
quests.why: Too many seedlings in one pot all grow weak. Fewer grow strong.
steps: Find a pot where the seedlings are crowded and touching.
Hold each one by a leaf, never the stem, and gently pull out or snip the weakest, so the rest have a finger’s width of space.
Water gently, and write in your diary how many you kept.

quests.title: Be the plant doctor: work out what a droopy plant needs
quests.why: Plants can’t say what’s wrong. Their leaves tell you instead.
steps: Find a plant at home that looks unhappy: droopy, yellow, leggy or crispy.
Check the clues: is the soil soggy or dry, is it leaning for the light, are there bugs under the leaves?
Make one change, write your diagnosis down, and check again in three days.

quests.title: Sow a new tray every week so there’s always something to pick
quests.why: Growers sow a little and often, so the harvest never runs out. It’s called succession sowing.
steps: Week one: sow a small tray of cress, mustard or pea shoots, and label it with the date.
Weeks two and three: sow another tray the same size.
Keep a rota of when each tray should be ready, so there’s always one to pick.

quests.title: Write a care card so anyone could look after your plant
quests.why: If you’re away for a night, your plant needs someone who knows what to do.
steps: Write what your plant needs: how much water, how often and how much light.
Add one warning sign to look out for, and what to do about it.
Teach someone at home your plant’s routine, then let them try it while you watch.

quests.title: Harvest day: share what you grew and tell its story
quests.why: Weeks of care, ready to share. The family sees what you grew, and how.
steps: Lay out your plant with your diary and your chart, like a little show.
Ask everyone about allergies first, then snip your crop with clean scissors and hand round a taste. Grew something that isn’t for eating? Show it off instead.
Tell everyone its story: how it started, the hardest bit and what you’d grow next.
